title: custom layer destroys mask when supports_masking = True
description:
Hi,

I am writing a model which masks time dimensions and then applies a dense layer over each non-masked dimension. I am finding that mask is destroyed by my custom layer implementation. Rather I expect the normal behaviour of layers with an opt in around masking to pass the mask through the layer. Below is a minimum working example of my implementation in the function API that fails on a custom layer wrapper around dense and and example that works using the core dense layer. I can work around by recalling `tf$keras$layers$Masking` on the output of the custom layer but for small batches and a relu activation function, this doesn't exclude the possibility of accidental masking. 
```
    ##custom layer
MyDenseLayer <- R6::R6Class(
  "CustomLayer",
  inherit = KerasLayer,
  
  public = list(
    num_outputs = NULL,
    kernel = NULL,
    supports_masking = T,
    
    initialize = function(num_outputs) {
      self$num_outputs <- num_outputs
    },
    
    build = function(input_shape) {
      self$kernel <- self$add_weight(name = 'kernel',
                                     shape = list(input_shape[[2]], self$num_outputs))
    },
    
    call = function(x, mask = NULL) {
      # tf$matmul(x, self$kernel)
      mask
    },
    
    compute_mask = function(x, mask = NULL) {
      mask
    },
    
    compute_output_shape = function(input_shape) {
      list(input_shape[[1]], self$num_outputs)
    }
  )
)

layer_my_dense <- function(object, num_outputs,name = NULL, trainable = TRUE) {
  create_layer(MyDenseLayer, object, list(
    num_outputs = as.integer(num_outputs),
    name = name,
    trainable = trainable
  ))
}


  #fails
inputs <- tf$keras$layers$Input(shape=list(10L))
maskingLayer = tf$keras$layers$Masking(mask_value=-9)
masked_input = maskingLayer(inputs)
custom_layer = layer_my_dense(num_outputs=5L)
custom_layer_output = custom_layer(masked_input)
custom_layer$input_mask
# KerasTensor(type_spec=TensorSpec(shape=(None,), dtype=tf.bool, name=None), name='masking_103/Squeeze:0')
custom_layer$output_mask
# NULL

#works
inputs <- tf$keras$layers$Input(shape=list(10L))
maskingLayer = tf$keras$layers$Masking(mask_value=-9)
masked_input = maskingLayer(inputs)
dense_layer = tf$keras$layers$Dense(5L)
dense_layer_output = dense_layer(masked_input)
dense_layer$input_mask
# KerasTensor(type_spec=TensorSpec(shape=(None,), dtype=tf.bool, name=None), name='masking_103/Squeeze:0')
dense_layer$output_mask
# KerasTensor(type_spec=TensorSpec(shape=(None,), dtype=tf.bool, name=None), name='Placeholder_1:0')
```

title: `tfruns` reports wrong results when using early stopping
description:
When using `tfruns` with `callbacks = callback_early_stopping(patience = 4, restore_best_weights = TRUE)` , a "wrong" set of results are reported since metrics come from the last epoch, when in fact the weights of the models are restored from a different epoch. Needless to say that the longer the patience, the more likely that your results may drastically differ.

![Untitled](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/47745523/120857721-0083f380-c582-11eb-8b10-4b95806f57d6.png)

This could be "manually" checked for a single run, but it is misleading when reviewing many runs (`ls_runs()`) and the choice of the best hyperparameters.

    layer_flatten() %>%

  CNN_model <- keras_model(input, output)
  
  #Compile model
    CNN_model %>% compile(
    loss = 'mse',
    optimizer = "adam", 
    metrics = c('mse', custom_metric('corr',metric_cor))
  )
  
  #Fit model
  history <- CNN_model %>% fit(
    Xtrain, ytrain, 
    epochs = 200,
    verbose = 0,
    batch_size = 32,
    validation_split = 0.2,
    callbacks = list(cp_callback)
  )
  
  CORMAX  <- max(history$metrics$val_corr, na.rm = T)
  if(CORMAX==Inf | CORMAX==-Inf) {CORMAX <- -1}

title: Transferring Python optimizer 'AdaMod' to Keras in R
description:
In [An Adaptive and Momental Bound Method for Stochastic Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.12249), a new optimizer `AdaMod` is being reported which is able to smooth out unexpected large learning rates throughout the training process. For details regarding its use in Python environments see [https://github.com/lancopku/AdaMod](https://github.com/lancopku/AdaMod). A recommended setting under these conditions is
```
optimizer = optim.AdaMod(
    m.parameters(),
    lr= 1e-3,
    betas=(0.9, 0.999),
    beta3=0.999,
    eps=1e-8,
    weight_decay=0,
)
```
Since I am working in RStudio with Keras in R, I tried to transfer `AdaMod` to my working `reticulate/conda` environment by following steps: 
```
library(keras)  
reticulate::py_install(c('adamod'), pip = TRUE)
```
which produced 
```
Requirement already up-to-date: adamod in c:\minico~1\envs\r-reti~1\lib\site-packages (0.0.3)
Requirement already satisfied, skipping upgrade: torch>=0.4.0 in c:\minico~1\envs\r-reti~1\lib\site-packages (from adamod) (1.4.0)
```
from which I gained some confidence to try `AdaMod` in one of my deep learning programs, configuring my model as I am used to do in case of Keras standard optimizers by specifying 
```
...
losslist <- list(output = 'kullback_leibler_divergence') 
metlist <- list(output = 'accuracy')
model %>% compile(AdaMod(m.parameters(), 
                        lr= 1e-3, 
                        betas=c(0.9, 0.999), 
                        beta3=0.999, 
                        eps=1e-8, 
                        weight_decay=0),
                  loss = losslist,
                  weighted_metrics = metlist)  
```
However, the disappointing result was
```
error in AdaMod(m.parameters(), lr = 0.001, betas = c(0.9, 0.999), beta3 = 0.999, ...:
   could not find function "AdaMod" 
Called from: compile.keras.engine.training.Model(., AdaMod(m.parameters(), 
    lr = 0.001, betas = c(0.9, 0.999), beta3 = 0.999, eps = 1e-08, 
    weight_decay = 0), loss = losslist, weighted_metrics = metlist)
```
The question obviously is, how could I proceed to get Keras in R to find and successfully apply this function?

Note: This problem was raised about a year ago in 
1. [How to install optimizer AdaMod into Keras/Reticulate virtual environment? #2](https://github.com/lancopku/AdaMod/issues/2) 
2.  as well as in [Transfer of a new Python optimizer to Keras in R, #1049](https://github.com/rstudio/keras/issues/1049)

but, unfortunately, is still pending unresolved. Any help would be highly appreciated.

title: Single custom Loss function for Multiple Output Regression not working
description:
Hi and thanks for the amazing community around Keras!

**What I am trying to do:** create a single custom Loss function to be optimized by a Multiple Output Regression.

**Problem**: while my attempts at customizing loss functions for Multiple Output Regression do seem to be working, Keras still seems to be calling the customized function for each output. There is no specific documentation on how to do this properly in the package documentation - so I have no idea whether this is a bug.

**What have I tried**: I tried dozens of different way to specify the custom loss function. Also, I have extensively searched online for related issues. There is a sheer amount of questions on this topic online, but nearly all about debugging similar problems with Keras directly within Python ([example 1](https://github.com/keras-team/keras/issues/13340), [example 2](https://github.com/keras-team/keras/issues/13654)). The few questions I found online about that when using the keras package remain unanswered even after years ([example 1](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/49992346/neural-network-for-regression-using-keras-in-r), [example 2](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/49992346/neural-network-for-regression-using-keras-in-r)).

**Reproducible Example**:

First I create some fake data so we can have a minimally reproducible example.

```
library(keras)
n <- 10000
k <- 4
x <- runif(n, -100, 100)
data <- data.frame()
for(i in 1:k)
{
    data[1:n,i] <- x + runif(n, -0.01, 0.01)
}
y1 <- apply(data, 1, function(x) median(as.numeric(x)))
y2 <- apply(data, 1, function(x) sd(as.numeric(x)))
targets <- data.frame(y1=y1, y2=y2)

cases <- sample(1:nrow(data), round(0.5*nrow(data)))
train_targets <- targets[cases,]
test_targets <- targets[-cases,]
train_data <- data[cases, ]
test_data <- data[-cases, ]
mean <- apply(train_data, 2, mean)
std <- apply(train_data, 2, sd)
train_data <- scale(train_data, center = mean, scale = std)
test_data <- scale(test_data, center = mean, scale = std)
```


Then, let's try a rather silly custom loss function just for the sake of example:
```
custom_loss <- function(y_pred, y_true)
{
    result <- abs(y_pred[1] - y_true[1]) * abs(y_pred[2] - y_true[2])
    return(result)
}
```

Finally, let's define the model and run it:

```
build_model <- function()
{
    input_tensor <- layer_input(shape = dim(train_data)[[2]])
    base_model <- input_tensor %>%
                    layer_dense(units = 64, activation = "relu") %>%
                    layer_dense(units = 64, activation = "relu")
    y1_prediction <- base_model %>% layer_dense(units = 1, name="y1")
    y2_prediction <- base_model %>% layer_dense(units = 1, name="y2")
    model <- keras_model(input_tensor, list(y1_prediction, y2_prediction))
    # model %>% compile(optimizer = "rmsprop", loss = list(y1="mse", y2="mse"))
    model %>% compile(optimizer = "rmsprop", loss = custom_loss)
}

model <- build_model()
history <- model %>% fit(train_data, list(as.numeric(train_targets$y1),
                                          as.numeric(train_targets$y2)),
                         epochs = 2, batch_size = 256, verbose = 1)
```


Result: I still get two loss function results, one for each output:

> Epoch 1/200
20/20 [==============================] - 2s 3ms/step - loss: 2266.0321 - y1_loss: 2265.9965 - y2_loss: 0.0357
Epoch 2/200
20/20 [==============================] - 0s 5ms/step - loss: 1795.3417 - y1_loss: 1795.3154 - y2_loss: 0.0264


Comparing the above code example with solutions implemented directly in Python, I would think it should have worked as is. In which case, the model still optimizing two losses may be a bug. If there is a proper specification to work around that, please let me know how could I correctly specify the model such as to have it optimize one single custom loss function to which the multiple predicted and true values are inputs?

title: Issue using custom generator at validation time (fit_generator)
description:
Hello the R deep learning community, 
It looks like I have to re-open [this issue](https://github.com/rstudio/keras/pull/1202#issue-599938073) related to #1201.
I just upgrade to keras 2.4.3 and tensorflow 2.4.1.
After doing this and testing a standard model of mine (Feature Pyramid Network with ResNet101 as pre-trained encoder) on a semantic segmentation task it looks like the behaviour of the model at validation time is incorrect, though training is behaving exactly as prior to upgrade. 

```

                                    shuffle = TRUE,
                                    intensity_operation = FALSE,
                                    batch_size = BATCH_SIZE)

val_generator <- custom_generator(data = val_input,
                                  shuffle = FALSE,
                                  intensity_operation = FALSE,
                                  batch_size = BATCH_SIZE)

history <- model %>% 
  fit_generator(
    generator = train_generator,
    epochs = EPOCHS,
    steps_per_epoch = STEPS_PER_EPOCHS,
    validation_data = val_generator,
    validation_steps = VALIDATION_STEPS,
    verbose = 1L
  )
```
Here is what I get after the model ran for 2 epochs (for testing):
```

title: Need to either automatically convert factors to character or numeric or give more informative error message.
description:
### To replicate: 

    foo <- keras_array(iris$Species);

### Expected behavior:

A NumPy array either of `str` or `number` objects

### Actual behavior: 

    Error in py_get_attr_impl(x, name, silent) : 
    AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'dtype'

If I wrap the input value either in `as.numeric()` or `as.character()` then `keras_array()` runs without error, so I guess it can handle discrete variables. Given that this is a package for helping R users use Keras and `factor` being  a very common data type in R, can `keras_array()` just detect `factor` variables and convert them to `character`.

The root cause seems to be that unlike a `character` or `numeric` array, for a `factor` array `r_to_py()` returns a `List` object, which lacks a `dtype` attribute, causing an error when you attempt to set that attribute here...

https://github.com/rstudio/keras/blob/09371e1cf2338a95f6cf42f11fc8ea944e9feeef/R/utils.R#L275-L276

If there are reasons you cannot auto-convert `factor` variables to `character`, can you at least catch this case and give an error message advising the user to do the conversion themselves? The current error message has no obvious connection to the workaround.

I was hoping to experiment with a non-negative constraint on the embedding matrix, but adding this constraint to the embedding layer in the tutorial makes fitting the model error out. 

```R
#download.file("https://snap.stanford.edu/data/finefoods.txt.gz", "finefoods.txt.gz")


library(readr)
library(stringr)

reviews <- reviews[str_sub(reviews, 1, 12) == "review/text:"]

reviews <- iconv(reviews, to = "UTF-8")

library(keras)

tokenizer <- text_tokenizer(num_words = 20000)
tokenizer %>% fit_text_tokenizer(reviews)

library(reticulate)
library(purrr)
skipgrams_generator <- function(text, tokenizer, window_size, negative_samples) {
  gen <- texts_to_sequences_generator(tokenizer, sample(text))
  function() {
    skip <- generator_next(gen) %>%
      skipgrams(
        vocabulary_size = tokenizer$num_words, 
        window_size = window_size, 
        negative_samples = 1
      )
    x <- transpose(skip$couples) %>% map(. %>% unlist %>% as.matrix(ncol = 1))
    y <- skip$labels %>% as.matrix(ncol = 1)
    list(x, y)
  }
}

model %>% compile(loss = "binary_crossentropy", optimizer = "adam")

title: Masking layer_repeat_vector in LSTM autoencoder
description:
I am building an LSTM autoencoder in R keras with different timestep inputs. As ragged tensors are not implemented yet I opted for masking shorter length inputs. The problem I'm facing is in the bottleneck layer where the layer_repeat_vector destroys the masking.

I found this helpful solution https://stackoverflow.com/a/59313862/4601329, and I'm trying to translate the Second Solution of the answer.

Here's my code:
```
library(keras)

# custom lstm bottleneck layer to keep masking after layer_repeat_vector
lstm_with_mask <- R6::R6Class("lstm_with_mask",
                              
                              inherit = KerasLayer,
                              
                              public = list(
                                
                                lstm_units = NULL,
                                in_shp = NULL,    # c(timesteps, features)
                                activation = NULL,
                                
                                initialize = function(lstm_units = NULL,
                                                      in_shp = NULL,
                                                      activation = NULL) {
                                  
                                  
                                  self$lstm_units <- lstm_units
                                  self$in_shp <- in_shp
                                  self$activation <- activation
                                  # self$lstm_layer <- layer_lstm(units = lstm_units, input_shape = in_shp, activation = activation, return_sequences = FALSE)
                                  # self$repeat_layer <- layer_repeat_vector(n=in_shp[1])   # timestep
                                },
                                
                                compute_mask = function(input, input_mask=NULL) {
                                  return(input_mask)
                                },
                                
                                call = function(x, mask = NULL) {
                                  
                                  l1 <- layer_lstm(units = self$lstm_units, input_shape = self$in_shp, activation = self$activation, return_sequences = FALSE)
                                  l2 <- layer_repeat_vector(n=self$in_shp[1])   # timestep

                                  return(l2(l1(x)))
                                  # return(self$repeat_layer(self$lstm_layer(x)))
                                }
                              )
)

# define layer wrapper function
layer_lstm_with_mask <- function(object, lstm_units = NULL,
                                 in_shp = NULL,    # c(timesteps, features)
                                 activation = NULL,
                                 name = 'lstm_with_mask') {
  create_layer(lstm_with_mask, object, list(lstm_units =  lstm_units, 
                                            in_shp = in_shp, 
                                            activation = activation,
                                            name = name
  ))
}


model <- keras_model_sequential()
model %>%
  layer_masking(mask_value = -9999,input_shape = c(timesteps_var, features)) %>%
  layer_lstm(units = 100, input_shape = c(timesteps_var, features), activation='relu', return_sequences = TRUE) %>%
  layer_lstm_with_mask(lstm_units = 50, in_shp = c(timesteps_var, features), activation='relu')
```
but if I check the masking with
```
for (ll in model$layers){
  cat('\n-----')
  print(ll$name)

  print(ll$output_mask)
}
```
I get
```

so the masking is still lost.

I think the problem is in defining the LSTM and RepeatVector inside `call` so that the edited `compute_mask` (explicitly returning the mask) doesn't affect the results. The proper way should be initializing both in the `initialize` function, but if I use the commented commands I get the following error
`Error in self$lstm_layer <- layer_lstm(units = lstm_units, input_shape = in_shp, : cannot add bindings to a locked environment`

  tseries <- target[-(1:N),]
  return(tseries)
}

 

##############################################################
#########""" Return training dataset with lag

title: load_model_tf with custom loss require the dict() function
description:
I put this here if someone else run into the trouble, it is more problem of documentation. 

I created a model with a custom loss function : 

```
smoothie <- function(y_true,y_pred){
    tf$losses$categorical_crossentropy(y_true, y_pred, label_smoothing=0.3)
}
```
Which make me think that the categorical_crossentropy function of the package keras could be updated too, to reflect the one of the python version of keras, which can use label_smoothing.

Running the following would create an error : 

`model <- load_model_tf("../input/efficientnetb7-label-smoothing-imagenet/EfficientB7_image_net/")
`
> ValueError: ('Unknown loss function', ':smoothie')

And this is when things began to be puzzling. Looking at https://github.com/keras-team/keras/issues/5916 in the main keras, it appeared to me that I must use custom_objects. But the documentation is totally clueless about how and using standard R data-structure did not worked (I tried a list without success). Finally looking at the solution provided on github, and the code of the function of the github repository, I remembered that there is some conversion to the dictionary format via reticulate, and indeed there is a function to do it. Using : 

`model <- load_model_tf("../input/efficientnetb7-label-smoothing-imagenet/EfficientB7_image_net/", custom_objects = dict(smoothie = "smoothie"))`

Worked perfectly.

I would suggest an update to the documentation or a way to pass a list as an argument, which the first logical attempt of a R user.

Sergio

title: Ubuntu 20.04 -> R-4.0.3 -> Keras -> Tensorflow -> CUDA -> Quadro GP100
description:
Sorry for asking yet another toolchain compatibility question, but I'm stymied by so many "moving parts", and I hope someone can point me in the right direction.  For years I have successfully run some Intel Xeon-based workstations (mostly offline) with Ubuntu 16.04 LTS, R, python 3.6, keras, tensorflow, and cuda (for my machine with the GPU). Now I wish to \move up to Ubuntu 20.04 and have set aside a test machine to see if I can get the whole toolchain working again. So far I seem to have Ubuntu 20.04.1 and R (I maintain my own R installation in /usr/local/) working pretty well. The missing pieces are keras, tensorflow, and cuda. On my Ubuntu 16.04 systems I had my own python 3.6 and cuda 10.0 installations. I was hoping that on Ubuntu 20.04, I could use the system versions of these: python 3.8 and cuda 10.1, but I ran into problems. For example, trying to import keras into python3 produces:

python3
Python 3.8.5 (default, Jul 28 2020, 12:59:40) 
[GCC 9.3.0] on linux
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>> import keras
Using TensorFlow backend.
2021-01-13 13:39:20.195264: W tensorflow/stream_executor/platform/default/dso_loader.cc:60] Could not load dynamic library 'libcudart.so.11.0'; dlerror: libcudart.so.11.0: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory
2021-01-13 13:39:20.195294: I tensorflow/stream_executor/cuda/cudart_stub.cc:29] Ignore above cudart dlerror if you do not have a GPU set up on your machine.
>>> 

So I gather that tensorflow 2.4.0, which python 3.8 installed, wants cuda 11.0, not the cuda 10.1 toolkit that comes with Ubuntu 20.04. From my researches on the web it also seems that earlier versions of tensorflow like 1.14.0 (which I use on my Ubuntu 16.04 machines), are not compatible with python 3.8. If I give up on trying to use python 3.8 and just go back to manually installing and maintaining python 3.6, with its keras and tensorflow versions, I could probably get everything working. But is there a better and simpler way to get an R and keras toolchain going on Ubuntu 20.04 that will support my Nvidia Quadro GP100 GPU?

Thanks for any help.

clean_lines <- function(lines){
  lines <- utf8_normalize(lines)
  lines <- remove_nonAlphanumericChar(lines)
  trimws(lines)
  lines <- add_space_before_punc(lines)
  lines<-tolower(lines)
  line <- split_in_Line(lines)
  
}

split_in_Line <- function(lines){
  str_split(lines,"\n")
}
add_space_before_punc <- function(lines){
  str_replace_all(lines,"([?.!])", "\\1")
}
remove_nonAlphanumericChar <- function(lines){
  str_replace_all(lines, "[[:punct:]]", " ")
}

encode_seq <- function(tokenizer, maxlength, lines){
  integerFromSeq <- tokenizer$texts_to_sequences(lines) 
  integerFromSeq <- pad_sequences(integerFromSeq, maxlen = maxlength, padding="post")
  return(integerFromSeq)
}
encoder_output <- function(sequence, vocabulary){

  for (i in sequence) {
    encoded <- to_categorical(i, num_classes=vocabulary)

  }
  arrOutput <- array(unlist(auxlist),dim =c(nrow(sequence),ncol(sequence),vocabulary))

}

get_longest <- function(dataset){
  pos <-0
  maxlen <- 0

    if(nchar(i)>maxlen){
      pos <-iter
      maxlen <- nchar(i)
    }
    iter <- iter+1
  }
  return(maxlen)

}
```

title: Weight pruning in Keras for R
description:
Weight pruning seems to be a valuable tool to improve neural networks' ability to generalize by throwing away those parts (weights) of the network which do not significantly contribute to convergence and accuracy. An introductory article can be found under [Obtaining Top Neural Network Performance Without Any Training](https://medium.com/analytics-vidhya/obtaining-top-neural-network-performance-without-any-training-5af0af464c59) and references given therein.

Unfortunately I cannot find any useful tools among the help pages of my Keras 2.3.0.0. package in R. Are there any other helpful packages or ready-to-use workarounds somewhere else to apply the technique of weight pruning (structured or unstructured) within Keras for R?

Any helpful hints would be highly appreciated.

title: Create custom metrics using R functions
description:
Hi,

I am interested in making a custom metric to compute AUC at the end of each batch (rather than computing accuracy). I have already figured out how to set up a callback using `callback_lambda()` to compute AUC `on_epoch_end`...

```r
# This works as a callback
auc <- vector("numeric")
callback_auc <- callback_lambda(
  on_epoch_end = function(batch, logs) {
    epoch_auc <- yardstick::roc_auc_vec(yy, predict(model, xx))
    auc <<- c(auc, epoch_auc)
  }
)
```

But I was hoping to compute AUC as a custom metric instead by supplying it to `compile(..., metric = auc)`. It seems like something like this should work for creating the custom metric:
```r
auc <- custom_metric("auc", function(y_true, y_pred) {yardstick::roc_auc_vec(y_true, y_pred)})

model %>% compile(
  optimizer = 'rmsprop',
  loss = 'categorical_crossentropy',
  metric = auc
)
```

But it fails. Besides the fact that `{yardstick}` requires `y_true` to be a factor, I believe the salient issue is that `y_true` and `y_pred` are returned as `tensorflow` tensors and not `R` vectors, and I am really not sure how to handle these tensors when trying to use `R` functions. Any guidance on how to create a custom metric which use R functions internally?

title: Changing learning rate and drop_out values of a model 'on the fly'.
description:
**Background**
In the past, methods for adapting learning rates have been an active area of research going from continuously varying learning rates to the extreme of using just one very high constant learning rate to achieve what the authors call super convergence in [arXiv:1708.07120v3 ](https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.07120); see this paper for further use cases and methods. 

**Motivations for changing network parameters**
The objective in these cases is, most frequently, improving convergence in case of one given, but often extremely large data set. The case of _rolling prediction or classification_, however, poses similar problems even in case of much smaller _data sets whose statistical properties may change considerably over time_. Just including the newly arrived data into the existing data pool doesn't seem to be appropriate, since it may take an amount of approx. the same size as the already existing data to avoid discrimination of the new properties; i.e. the adaptive process is rather slow. 

**Known options to do parameter changes under Keras for R**
A rolling prediction may require different values for several parameters like learning rate `LRate` in the optimizer, `drop_out` values in particular layers and/or `model_weights` of the whole model. While it is perfectly simple to `set_weights` in a given model betwen two training cycles, to my knowledge (and based on Keras 2.3, Tensorflow 2.2, Reticulate 1.16), changing `LRate` requires subsequent application of the `compile()` command; changing `drop_out` values requires a complete read-in of the model and, again, the `compile()` command. The execution of the `compile()` command as well as reading-in of the whole network structure requires a relatively long time which may become prohibitive in case of more frequent adaptation of these parameters.

**My question**
Are there any options to shorten or, rather, to accelerate  these procedures, e.g. by commands similar to `set_weights`, somewhere on the Tensorflow level or by individually designed custom functions? Thank you in advance for any suitable hints!

**Note added 28 September 2020** 
I just discovered [adtune](https://github.com/awslabs/adatune), a fairly new optimizer designed to tune hyperparameters and, in particular, the learning rate. How could one transfer that to proper use within Keras for R?

title: TF 2.3: error when calling plot.keras_training_history
description:
Hi,

I get the following error when I call plot (i.e., plot.keras_training_history) on a keras_training_history object in TF 2.3.

```
> plot(history)
Error in data.frame(epoch = seq_len(x$params$epochs), value = unlist(values),  : 
  arguments imply differing number of rows: 100, 132, 400
```

History is the object returned by fit.keras.engine.training.Model. The last 3 numbers depend on the (maximum) number of epochs (above example: 100) and the number of epochs that the model was actually trained for (above example: training was early terminated after 33 epochs; 33 * 4 = 132).

Anirban

title: Error in py_call_impl(callable, dots$args, dots$keywords) :    RuntimeError: tf.gradients is not supported when eager execution is enabled. Use tf.GradientTape instead.
description:
Hi, I have run sample code with 'Deep learning with R' code below.
(
however, k_gradient() function below is not working with error messages.
error code is : grads <- k_gradients(loss, dream)[[1]] 

 Error in py_call_impl(callable, dots$args, dots$keywords) : 
  RuntimeError: tf.gradients is not supported when eager execution is enabled. Use tf.GradientTape instead. 

someone help me? gradienttape() function is not in KerasR.
my environments are: windows 10, No GPU, R 4.0, RStudio 1.3.1056, KerasR with Anaconda 3 with python 3.7.


library(keras)
k_set_learning_phase(0) 

model <- application_inception_v3(  
  weights = "imagenet",    
  include_top = FALSE,      
)

layer_contributions <- list(
  mixed2 = 0.2,
  mixed3 = 3,
  mixed4 = 2,
  mixed5 = 1.5
)

layer_dict <- model$layers
names(layer_dict) <- lapply(layer_dict, function(layer) layer$name) 
loss <- k_variable(0) 
for (layer_name in names(layer_contributions)) {
  coeff <- layer_contributions[[layer_name]]
  activation <- layer_dict[[layer_name]]$output
  scaling <- k_prod(k_cast(k_shape(activation), "float32"))
  loss <- loss + (coeff * k_sum(k_square(activation)) / scaling)
}
dream <- model$input 
grads <- k_gradients(loss, dream)[[1]] 

grads <- grads / k_maximum(k_mean(k_abs(grads)), 1e-7) 
outputs <- list(loss, grads)
fetch_loss_and_grads <- k_function(list(dream), outputs) 
eval_loss_and_grads <- function(x) {
  outs <- fetch_loss_and_grads(list(x))
  loss_value <- outs[[1]]
  grad_values <- outs[[2]]
  list(loss_value, grad_values)
}
gradient_ascent <- function(x, iterations, step, max_loss = NULL) {
  for (i in 1:iterations) {
    c(loss_value, grad_values) %<-% eval_loss_and_grads(x)
    if (!is.null(max_loss) && loss_value > max_loss)
      break
    cat("...Loss value at", i, ":", loss_value, "\n")
    x <- x + (step * grad_values)
  }
  x
}

resize_img <- function(img, size) {
  image_array_resize(img, size[[1]], size[[2]])
}
save_img <- function(img, fname) {
  img <- deprocess_image(img)
  image_array_save(img, fname)
}
preprocess_image <- function(image_path) {
  image_load(image_path) %>% 
    image_to_array() %>% 
    array_reshape(dim = c(1, dim(.))) %>% 
    inception_v3_preprocess_input()
}
deprocess_image <- function(img) {
  img <- array_reshape(img, dim = c(dim(img)[[2]], dim(img)[[3]], 3))
  img <- img / 2
  img <- img + 0.5
  img <- img * 255
  
  dims <- dim(img)
  img <- pmax(0, pmin(img, 255))
  dim(img) <- dims
  img
}

step <- 0.01          # Gradient ascent step size
num_octave <- 3       # Number of scales at which to run gradient ascent
octave_scale <- 1.4   # Size ratio between scales
iterations <- 20      # Number of ascent steps per scale
max_loss <- 10  
dir.create("dream")
base_image_path <- "Downloads/creative_commons_elephant.jpg"
img <- preprocess_image(base_image_path)
original_shape <- dim(img)[-1]
successive_shapes <- list(original_shape)
for (i in 1:num_octave) { 
  shape <- as.integer(original_shape / (octave_scale ^ i))
  successive_shapes[[length(successive_shapes) + 1]] <- shape 
}
successive_shapes <- rev(successive_shapes) 
original_img <- img 
shrunk_original_img <- resize_img(img, successive_shapes[[1]])
for (shape in successive_shapes) {
  cat("Processsing image shape", shape, "\n")
  img <- resize_img(img, shape)
  img <- gradient_ascent(img,

  upscaled_shrunk_original_img <- resize_img(shrunk_original_img, shape)
  same_size_original <- resize_img(original_img, shape)
  lost_detail <- same_size_original - upscaled_shrunk_original_img
  
  img <- img + lost_detail
  shrunk_original_img <- resize_img(original_img, shape)
  save_img(img, fname = sprintf("dream/at_scale_%s.png",
                                paste(shape, collapse = "x")))

title: multi_gpu_model documentation does not reflect its deprecation / removal

title: Manipulating model weights in Keras for R
description:
The Keras-for-R command `get_weights(object)` produces a list of different R arrays for all weights of a model. There is a corresponding command `set_weights(object)` permitting the (re-) insertion of this list of weights into the model, e.g. after some manipulation of the list items. However, since the list items usually are arrays of different shapes, it is not possible e.g. simply to add two lists (of same structure, of course) or to multiply one given list by a common factor.

I know there are tf-commands for these operations in Python, i.e. for manipulating weight tensors in particular. Are there any means to use these commands in Keras for R?  As indicated above, I am particularly interested in adding and scaling weight tensors.

title: Keras tries do reinstall tensorflow when I only have the cpu version installed
description:
Hi, 

We are working on servers with no GPU. Hence, our users use the CPU version of tensorflow. 

What we did to install is 
```r
library(tensorflow)
install_tensorflow(envname="r-tensorflow",
                   version = "cpu",
                   python = "/applis/Python/3.6.10/bin/python3", 
                   ignore_installed = FALSE)
```
Everything is fine and we get `tensorflow-cpu` installed. 
```bash
Collecting tensorflow-cpu==2.2.0
```

But when trying to test the installation with the keras tutorial

```r
library(keras)
# load data (we are on offline servers so they are cached)
c(c(x_train, y_train), c(x_test, y_test)) %<-% dataset_mnist(path = "/home/share/echange/data/mnist.npz")
```
keras will reinstall `tensorflow` 
```r
Using virtual environment '/home/bureau.si.interne/dervieuxchr/.virtualenvs/r-tensorflow' ...
Looking in indexes: https://devin-depot.rte-france.com/repository/pypi-all/simple
Collecting tensorflow
```

Looking with `pip list` in the virtualenv I have both
```r
tensorflow                2.2.0
tensorflow-cpu         2.2.0
```

This will cause `tensorflow` to be used, and I have what I think to be GPU related errors. 

With `tensorflow-cpu` only, everything is working fine. 

note that this happens only the first time I use 
```r
c(c(x_train, y_train), c(x_test, y_test)) %<-% dataset_mnist(path = "/home/share/echange/data/mnist.npz")
```
in a R session. 

I don't really know what happens 🤔 Is there a check somewhere for tensorflow when fist executing a Keras function ?

title: Scipy requirement is not correct for the tensorflow that install_keras download
description:
While using this simple function in R 3.6.2 on linux centos7
```r
library(keras)
install_keras(envname = "r-keras")
```
the installation went well but I got this error
```bash
ERROR: tensorflow 2.2.0 has requirement scipy==1.4.1; python_version >= "3", but you'll have scipy 1.5.0 which is incompatible.
```

`install_keras` will ask to install `scipy`
https://github.com/rstudio/keras/blob/cdbfaaaa293eea5a8842921556b3ebd7a16b1ba5/R/install.R#L144-L152
without any version requirement but then, tensorflow will install using `install_tensorflow` and it will default to 2.2 
https://github.com/rstudio/tensorflow/blob/9a035f4832feeaf792ac8e708cde5db8419a19d6/R/install.R#L87 since the 11 may (https://github.com/rstudio/tensorflow/commit/afd245de1883c412fc6260c35cd81e5047f3a22f)

However, tensorflow seems to use `scipy==1.4.1` as requirement (https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/d8c49c2fdeed114470e2773967dddb932e9a9fb3/tensorflow/tools/pip_package/setup.py#L73)

So if I do first tensorflow, then keras, the already 1.4.1 installed scipy is replaced by 1.5 (I thought it would keep the one found though 🤔 )
```r
library(tensorflow)
# will install scipy 1.4.1
install_tensorflow(envname="r-tensorflow", ignore_installed = FALSE)
library(keras)
# will replace by last version (1.5 now) and throw the error
install_keras(envname = "r-tensorflow")
```

I don't if this as an impact on anything, but as a user getting this error is questionning. I used this afterward to be sure to have the correct version
```r
reticulate::py_install("scipy==1.4.1", envname = "r-tensorflow")
```

Maybe something could be done in keras to respect the tensorflow requirements ?

title: Possible bug in default implementation of 'mean_squared_error' (MSE) loss function in Keras.
description:
In the Boston Housing Prices regression tutorial, I tested the default model and noted an apparent source of instability in the model.

I looked into it, and figured out that the last batch only has 3 samples. When I started tracking the loss of each batch, I noted that the loss of the last batch was a factor of approximately 11 greater than the losses of all other batches (plot below).

This makes sense, since 11 is roughly equal to the ratio of the default batch size to the last batch size (32/3 = 10.67). However, I've been poking around in the keras/tf backend and it's unclear whether or not the loss of the last batch is ever adjusted/scaled prior to computing the gradients.

As an empirical test, I built a sum of squared errors loss function (MSE except I skipped the last step of calculating the mean) and applied it to the dataset. The result was apparent and significant improvement in the model, which leads me to believe that the unadjusted last batch loss is causing the model to overfit and become unstable (plots also below).

Basically, I'm posing 2 questions:
1) Does the default implementation of MSE scale/adjust the loss of the last batch prior to computing the gradients?
2) Either way, can someone point me to the exact place(s) in the code where the loss is used to compute the gradient?

Thanks!

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/30445407/85391271-cb140080-b4fe-11ea-8212-9532646fd0cc.png)

Hi! I am training an LSTM model. I am using the following data generator proposed in the time series tutorial by F. Chollet and J. J. allaire :
```
lookback <- 21
step <- 3
batch_size <- 128
delay <- 1

generator <- function(data, lookback, delay, min_index, max_index, shuffle = FALSE, batch_size, step) {
  if (is.null(max_index))
    max_index <- nrow(data) - delay - 1
  i <- min_index + lookback
  function() {
    if (shuffle) {
      rows <- sample(c((min_index+lookback):max_index), size = batch_size)
    } else {
      if (i + batch_size >= max_index)
        i <<- min_index + lookback
      rows <- c(i:min(i+batch_size-1, max_index))
      i <<- i + length(rows)
    }
    
    samples <- array(0, dim = c(length(rows), lookback / step, dim(data)[[-1]]))
    targets <- array(0, dim = c(length(rows)))
    
    for (j in 1:length(rows)) {
      indices <- seq(rows[[j]] - lookback, rows[[j]]-1, length.out = dim(samples)[[2]])
      samples[j,,] <- data[indices,] 
      targets[[j]] <- data[rows[[j]] + delay, 4]
      }  
    
    list(samples, targets)
  }
}
```

      dif2  <- y_true - k_mean(y_true)
      squ2  <- k_pow(dif2, 2)
      sum2  <- k_sum(squ2)
      
      L <- sum1/sum2
      
      return(L)

title: `to_categorical` should handle factor and character vectors
description: `to_categorical` expects integer vector from 0 to `n-1`. Some beginner users are not aware of it (certainly my students, see also https://github.com/rstudio/keras/issues/53), maybe it makes sense to have some special handling for factor/character vector before calling `keras.utils.to_categorical`.

title: Memory leak when writing custom callback
description:
The code in this example allocates an increasing amount of memory after every epoch.

```
library(magrittr)
library(keras)
model <- keras::keras_model_sequential()
model %>% 
  layer_dense(units = 4, activation = 'relu', input_shape = c(5)) %>% 
  layer_dense(units = 3, activation = 'softmax')

model %>% compile(
  loss = 'categorical_crossentropy',
  optimizer = keras::optimizer_rmsprop(),
  metrics = c('accuracy')
)

dummy_generator <- function(batch_size){
  function(){
    x <- sample(0:4, batch_size ,replace = TRUE)
    x <- keras::to_categorical(x, num_classes = 5)
    y <- sample(0:2, batch_size ,replace = TRUE)
    y <- keras::to_categorical(y, num_classes = 3)
    list(x,y)
  }
}

gen <- dummy_generator(batch_size=7)  
gen_val <- dummy_generator(batch_size=7)  

cb <- R6::R6Class("cb",
                  inherit = keras::KerasCallback,
                  
                  public = list(
                    
                    on_epoch_end = function(epoch, logs) {
                      
                      input <- array(1:5, dim = c(1,5))
                      for (i in 1:50){
                        pred <- self$model$predict(input)
                      }
                      
                    }
                  ))

custom_cb <- cb$new()

model %>% keras::fit_generator(
  generator = gen,
  validation_data = gen_val,
  validation_steps = 2,
  steps_per_epoch = 15,
  epochs = 150,
  callbacks = list(custom_cb)
)
```

title: Trouble in implementing a custom loss: ValueError: Dimensions must be equal, but are 31 and 32
description:
Hi,

I am trying to implement a custom loss function for a real-valued outcome and a predicted vector of probabilities of bins (essentially an alternative to the cross-entropy loss). 

**Edit** Upon re-reading the documentation for custom loss function, I realized that my initial error may have been that `y_true` and `y_pred` need to be tensors of equal shape in the loss function. I have added a second example below, which leads to different errors, though.

Here is the **first attempt/version**

Example code with simulation data:

```
rm(list=ls())

library(keras)

n <- 5000
x <- matrix(rnorm(5*n, 0, 1), nrow = n)
beta1 <- matrix(rnorm(5*n, 0, 1), nrow = n)

y <- apply(x * beta1, 1, sum) 

my_bin_edges <- seq(-15, 16, 1)
y[y <= -15] <- -15
y[y > 16] <- 16

ind_train <- 1:(n-1000)
ind_test <- (max(ind_train)+1):n

x_train <- x[ind_train,]
x_test <- x[ind_test,]

y_train <- y[ind_train]
y_test <- y[ind_test]

my_loss <- function(y_true, y_pred, bin_edges = my_bin_edges){
  
  nb <- length(bin_edges)
  left_k <- k_constant(bin_edges[1:(nb-1)])
  right_k <- k_constant(bin_edges[2:nb])
  
  z_k <- k_cast_to_floatx(k_all(list(k_less_equal(left_k, y_true), k_less_equal(y_true, right_k)), axis = 1)) * y_true + 
    k_cast_to_floatx(k_all(list(k_less_equal(right_k, y_true), k_greater(y_true, left_k)), axis = 1)) * right_k + 
    k_cast_to_floatx(k_all(list(k_less_equal(y_true, left_k), k_less(y_true, right_k)), axis = 1)) * left_k
  
  min_left_k <- k_constant(bin_edges[1])
  max_right_k <- k_max(right_k)

  z_transf_k <- z_k +
    k_cast_to_floatx(k_less(y_true, min_left_k)) * (y_true * k_ones_like(left_k) - z_k) * k_concatenate(list(k_ones(c(1)),k_zeros(c(length(left_k) - 1)))) +
    k_cast_to_floatx(k_greater(y_true, max_right_k)) * (y_true * k_ones_like(left_k) - z_k) * k_concatenate(list(k_zeros(c(length(left_k) - 1)), k_ones(c(1))))

  L_k <- k_gather(k_cumsum(k_concatenate(list(k_zeros_like(y_true), y_pred))), 1:(length(left_k)))
  U_k <- k_ones(c(length(left_k)) )- k_cumsum(y_pred)

  w_k <- (z_transf_k - left_k) / (right_k - left_k)

  punif_w_k <- k_clip(w_k, 0, 1)
  k_sum((right_k - left_k) * (k_abs(w_k - punif_w_k) + 
                                (k_ones(c(length(left_k))) - L_k - U_k) * k_square(punif_w_k) - 
                                punif_w_k * (k_ones(c(length(left_k))) - k_constant(2)*L_k) + 
                                k_square((k_ones(c(length(left_k))) - L_k - U_k)) / k_constant(3) + 
                                (k_ones(c(length(left_k))) - L_k) * U_k))
}

model <- keras_model_sequential() 
model %>% 
  layer_dense(units = 100, activation = 'relu', input_shape = c(5)) %>% 
  layer_dense(units = length(my_bin_edges) - 1, activation = 'softmax')

model %>% compile(
  optimizer = optimizer_adam(),
  metrics = c('accuracy'),
  loss = function(y_true, y_pred)
    my_loss(y_true, y_pred, bin_edges = my_bin_edges)
)

summary(model)

history <- model %>% fit(
  x_train, y_train,
  epochs = 10, batch_size = 1024,
  validation_split = 0.2
)
```

Executing this results in the following error message:

```
 Error in py_call_impl(callable, dots$args, dots$keywords) : 
  RuntimeError: Evaluation error: ValueError: Dimensions must be equal, but are 31 and 32 for 'loss/dense_115_loss/Sub_7' (op: 'Sub') with input shapes: [31], [31,32]..
```
I am unsure how to debug the model / loss. In particular, where do the shaoes [31,32] come from, and what does the (op: 'Sub') indicate?


... and here is the **second attempt/version**, now adjusted by converting `y_true` into a tensor of the same shape as `y_pred` first, by using `to_categorical`: The simulation example is slightly modified, but this shouldn't matter.

```
rm(list=ls())

library(keras)

n <- 5000
x <- matrix(rnorm(5*n, 0, 1), nrow = n) + 2
beta1 <- matrix(rnorm(5*n, 0, 1), nrow = n) + 2

y <- apply(x * beta1, 1, sum) 

summary(y)

    k_cast_to_floatx(k_all(list(k_less_equal(right_k, y_k), k_greater(y_k, left_k)), axis = 1)) * right_k + 
    k_cast_to_floatx(k_all(list(k_less_equal(y_k, left_k), k_less(y_k, right_k)), axis = 1)) * left_k
  
  min_left_k <- k_constant(bin_edges[1])
  max_right_k <- k_max(right_k)
  
  z_transf_k <- z_k +
    k_cast_to_floatx(k_less(y_k, min_left_k)) * (y_k * k_ones_like(left_k) - z_k) * k_concatenate(list(k_ones(c(1)),k_zeros(c(length(left_k) - 1)))) +
    k_cast_to_floatx(k_greater(y_k, max_right_k)) * (y_k * k_ones_like(left_k) - z_k) * k_concatenate(list(k_zeros(c(length(left_k) - 1)), k_ones(c(1))))

  L_k <- k_gather(k_cumsum(k_concatenate(list(k_zeros(c(1)), y_pred))), 1:(length(left_k)))
  U_k <- k_ones(c(length(left_k))) - k_cumsum(y_pred)

  w_k <- (z_transf_k - left_k) / (right_k - left_k)

  punif_w_k <- k_clip(w_k, 0, 1)
  k_sum((right_k - left_k) * (k_abs(w_k - punif_w_k) +
                                (k_ones(c(length(left_k))) - L_k - U_k) * k_square(punif_w_k) -
                                punif_w_k * (k_ones(c(length(left_k))) - k_constant(2)*L_k) +
                                k_square((k_ones(c(length(left_k))) - L_k - U_k)) / k_constant(3) +
                                (k_ones(c(length(left_k))) - L_k) * U_k))
}

model <- keras_model_sequential() 
model %>% 
  layer_dense(units = 100, activation = 'relu', input_shape = c(5)) %>% 
  layer_dense(units = length(my_bin_edges) - 1, activation = 'softmax')

model %>% compile(
  optimizer = optimizer_adam(),
  metrics = c('accuracy'),
  loss = function(y_true, y_pred)
    my_loss(y_true, y_pred, bin_edges = my_bin_edges)
)

summary(model)

history <- model %>% fit(
  x_train, y_train,

title: Transfer of a new Python optimizer to Keras in R
description:
Important progress has been made in developing adaptive optimizers which are able to overcome the hurdle of oscillating between local optima, causing non-convergence problems and poor generalization performance. The challenge is beautifully illustrated by pictures devoted to [a collection of optimizers for Pytorch](https://pythonawesome.com/a-collection-of-optimizers-for-pytorch/), designed to overcome these problems.
I am particularly interested in the optimizer [adamod](https://github.com/lancopku/AdaMod) which has been investigated thoroughly [elsewhere](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.12249). It is easy to install and import this Python optimizer into the virtual environment established by Keras for R applying the usual simple process to transfer Python functions into this environment. In Python power shell,

```
conda activate r-reticulate
pip install adamod
``` 
installs adamod 0.0.3 into the virtual environment r-reticulate. An then, in Keras for R, with

```
library reticulate
optimizer_adamod <- import('adamod')
```
the import into R is readily done. The usual `compile()` function of Keras, however, does not recognize the newly defined `optimizer_adamod()` and its parameters. And this raises the question: How can I transform this optimizer into a form compatible with Keras for R?
Any hints would be highly appreciated!

title: Add name argument to keras_model function
description:
Could you add `name` argument to `keras_model` function ? For some reason it's possible to name only `Sequential` and `Custom` models in `R`, but not models created by `Functional API`:

```
Errror in 'keras_model(input, list(out1, out2, out3, out4), name = "my_model")':
  unused argument (name = "my_model")
```

It's a small thing but it would be useful when stacking models not layers on top of each other.

title: RStudio freezing after evaluate()
description:
I believe this is the same issue that was reported [here](https://github.com/rstudio/keras/issues/957), which was closed without resolution.

Running evaluate() on certain trained keras/TF models (example below) within RStudio results in QtWebEngineProc going to 100% and the system freezing for a solid ~5-10 minutes before finally returning the performance metric, as well as printing equal signs that fill up the entire console. When I run the exact same command in R on the cmd-line there is no freezing/lag and the evaluation executes immediately with no printing of equal signs.

I am using keras 2.2.5.0 with tensorflow 2.0.0 (CPU version).

Reproducible example:
```
library(keras)
library(tidyverse)

max_features <- 10000                                         
maxlen <- 20                                                  
imdb <- dataset_imdb(num_words = max_features)
c(c(x_train, y_train), c(x_test, y_test)) %<-% imdb           
x_train <- pad_sequences(x_train, maxlen = maxlen) # Restrict each entry to the first 20 words    
x_test <- pad_sequences(x_test, maxlen = maxlen)

model <- keras_model_sequential() %>%
  layer_embedding(input_dim = 10000, output_dim = 8,            
                  input_length = maxlen) %>%
  layer_flatten() %>%                                           
  layer_dense(units = 1, activation = "sigmoid")                
model %>% compile(
  optimizer = "rmsprop",
  loss = "binary_crossentropy",
  metrics = c("acc")
)
summary(model)
history <- model %>% fit(
  x_train, y_train,
  epochs = 10,
  batch_size = 32,
  validation_split = 0.2
)

model %>% evaluate(x_test, y_test)
```

title: LSTM poor prediction : big gap between loss and val loss
description:
I am training an lstm model that I constructed using Keras in R following the time series [forecasting tutorial ](https://blogs.rstudio.com/tensorflow/posts/2017-12-20-time-series-forecasting-with-recurrent-neural-networks/) by F. Chollet and J. J. Allaire. 
The problem that I have is that there is a huge gap between the training loss and the val_loss and they never converge and after some epochs they stop decreasing. The predictions that I get are very poor.

So I tried to adjust the model. I have tried different kinds of adaptations that had been proposed for similar problems, but with any success. Here is the list of the things that I have tried :
-test different train/validation/test split rates
-test different loss functions
-add/remove activation functions
-test different lookback and sampling step values
-test different optimizers
-test different momentum and decay values (while using sgd), clipping
-test different lr (learning rate) from 1e-6 to 0.1 : I finally saw that a lr value close to the default lr worked better.
-test different step per epochs value
-increase and decrease batch size
-test different structures with different degrees of complexity: in fact adding neither nodes nor layers improved predictions, so I kept the simple initial structure that I had. I also tried to use regularizers : recurrent drop out, drop out, initializers, ..

I know that I have to reduce the training loss (mae) at very early epochs to a level of 0.05 to get decent results. I would highly appreciate if anyone could suggest me a way to achieve this. Many thanks in advance for your time !

description:
Hi,

When using `hdf5_matrix()` and `flow_images_from_data()`, does the whole HDF5 file get loaded into memory when invoked during model fitting, or is it actually only `flow`ing data from the HDF5 file in batches? 

Is there a computational benefit for flowing batches from a HDF5 rather than trying to load the HDF5 into memory as an R array (assuming it can be loaded into memory)?

For example:

```r
library(keras)
library(rhdf5)

# HDF5 component
h5createFile('test.h5')
h5createGroup('test.h5', 'data')
# 100 images with dimension 100x100 (grayscale channel only)

)

hist <-

    flow_images_from_data(
      dx,
      dy %>% to_categorical(),

title: Incorrect conda environment information
description:
Description in `keras::install_keras` says the following:
>Keras and TensorFlow will be installed into an "r-tensorflow" virtual or conda environment.

However there is no default value set for `envname` parameter. This results in an installation inside the default `r-reticulate` environment, as mentioned on [R tensorflow page](https://tensorflow.rstudio.com/installation/#installation-methods). At the moment `envname` can be passed to the `tensorflow::install_tensorflow` through the ellipsis.

In the tensorflow package the default environment was changed in the [1.14.1 release](https://github.com/rstudio/tensorflow/blob/master/NEWS.md#tensorflow-1141-cran). Setting `envname = "r-tensorflow"` helps to avoid potential conflicts if some modules are already installed inside the default environment. However if the `r-reticulate` env is desired as standard one then the docs should be corrected.

Please let me know if you would like me to provide a PR.

title: Error with get_or_create_global_step in TF core API2.0
description:
Hi,
I'm trying to run the VAE example available in keras/vignettes/examples/eager_cvae.R, but I am running into a problem related to having Tensorflow Core 2.0 installed. I did overcome a few issues, that may be worth updating in the example file:

1) To avoid issues related to conversions from floats to doubles, I added this line at the start of the script:
tf$keras$backend$set_floatx('float64')

2) Setting the optimizer to be used had to be changed to:
optimizer <- tf$optimizers$Adam(1e-4)

But I am now stuck on an issue I jave not been able to resolve:

In the training loop there are calls on lines 288 and 292 to:

global_step = tf$train$get_or_create_global_step())

which results in the error:

Error: AttributeError: module 'tensorflow_core._api.v2.train' has no attribute 'get_or_create_global_step'

After some searching I first tried setting this manually:

global_step = tf$Variable(1, name='global_step')

but this generates another error:

Error in py_call_impl(callable, dots$args, dots$keywords) : 
  TypeError: apply_gradients() got an unexpected keyword argument 'global_step'

I also tried setting it using the experimental summary module:

global_step = tf$summary$experimental$get_step()

but got the same error. Does anyone have a simple (or even not so simple) solution for this problem?

Thanks!
Martin

title: Error with tensorflow 2:  Inputs to eager execution function cannot be Keras symbolic tensors
description:
Hi everyone,

I am running into a problem migrating my code from tensorflow 1 to tensorflow 2. 

Below is sample code for a training a model with a custom loss function for a binomial distribution (with arbitrary and sample-specific N) that works with tensorflow 1 but throws an error with tensorflow 2 in `keras::fit`:

```
Error in py_call_impl(callable, dots$args, dots$keywords) : 
  _SymbolicException: Inputs to eager execution function cannot be Keras symbolic tensors, but found [<tf.Tensor 'logNchooseK:0' shape=(None, 1) dtype=float32>, <tf.Tensor 'N:0' shape=(None, 1) dtype=float32>]
```

I am using keras input layers in my custom loss function as my loss function depends on additional information other than the predictors and observed values. In this example, the outside information are the number of trials for each observation (N) and the appropriate binomial coefficient for the likelihood/loss function that cannot easily computed with the keras helper functions (logNchooseK).

Could you please advise on how to accomplish this with tensorflow 2?

```{r}
library(dplyr)

# create conda environments with tensorflow 1 and 2
reticulate::conda_create(envname = "tfpython", packages = c("tensorflow=1"))
reticulate::conda_create(envname = "tf2python", packages = c("tensorflow=2"))

k = list(
  # set this to tf2pthon to reproduce the error
  # set it to tfpython to reproduce the functioning example
  # TODO restart your R session before changing the conda environment
  tfenv = "tf2python",
  seed = 12345,
  validation_split = .2
)

set.seed(k$seed)
reticulate::use_condaenv(k$tfenv)

# define network -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

predictors_layer = keras::layer_input(
  shape = 2,
  name = "predictors"
)

N_layer = keras::layer_input(
  shape = 1,
  name = "N"
)

logNchooseK_layer = keras::layer_input(
  shape = 1,
  name = "logNchooseK"
)

output_layer = keras::layer_dense(
  predictors_layer,
  units = 1,
  activation = "linear",
  name = "output"
)

# define model --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

binomial_loss = function(y_true, y_pred) {
  predicted_prob = keras::k_exp(y_pred) / (1 + keras::k_exp(y_pred))
  
  neg_loglik = -(logNchooseK_layer + y_true * keras::k_log(predicted_prob) +
    (N_layer - y_true) * keras::k_log(1 - predicted_prob))
  
  return(neg_loglik)
}

model = keras::keras_model(
  inputs = c(predictors_layer, N_layer, logNchooseK_layer),
  outputs = output_layer
)

keras::compile(
  model,
  loss = binomial_loss,
  optimizer = keras::optimizer_adam()
)

# train model ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

sample_data = tibble::tibble(
  var1 = rnorm(20),
  var2 = rnorm(20),
  N = sample(100, size = 20, replace = TRUE),
  true_prob = plogis(.5  * var1 + .75 * var2),
  outcome = rbinom(n = 20, size = N, prob = true_prob),
  logNchooseK = lchoose(N, outcome)
)

# this works with tensorflow 1 but crashes with tensorflow 2
keras::fit(
  model,
  x = list(
    predictors = sample_data %>%
      select(var1, var2) %>%
      mutate_all(as.double) %>%
      as.matrix(),
    N = sample_data %>%
      select(N) %>%
      mutate_all(as.double) %>%
      as.matrix(),
    logNchooseK = sample_data %>%
      select(logNchooseK) %>%
      mutate_all(as.double) %>%
      as.matrix()
  ),
  y = list(
    output = sample_data %>%
      select(outcome) %>%
      mutate_all(as.double) %>%
      as.matrix()
  ),
  validation_split = k$validation_split,
  view_metrics = TRUE,
  epochs = 1000
)

# evaluate model ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

predicted_probabilities = plogis(
  model$predict(
    x = list(
      predictors = sample_data %>%
        select(var1, var2) %>%
        mutate_all(as.double) %>%
        as.matrix(),
      N = sample_data %>%
        select(N) %>%
        mutate_all(as.double) %>%
        as.matrix(),
      logNchooseK = sample_data %>%
        select(logNchooseK) %>%
        mutate_all(as.double) %>%
        as.matrix()
    )
  )
)

plot(
  x = predicted_probabilities,
  y = sample_data$true_prob,
  col = ifelse(1:nrow(sample_data) < (1-k$validation_split) * nrow(sample_data), "red", "blue")
)
abline(a = 0, b = 1)
```

Your help is much appreciated. Thank you!

title: flow image from directory for U-net segmentation in r
description:
Hi, i am trying to use the flow_images_from_directory() function with the unet segmentation and i didn't manage to combine the image and mask generators, in python it seems that it is made with the function zip(). I have try with list() but it return the error ''Error in py_call_impl(callable, dots$args, dots$keywords) :   TypeError: 'list' object is not an iterator " when i run the training. Any suggestion ? i can make the data available it someone is interested. The images are of size 128x128x3 (rgb) and the masks 128x128x1.
___________________________________________________________________________________
update
i have now resolved this, the only problem now is that it can use only one worker or it gives this error "Error: You may not specify workers > 1 for R based generator functions (R generators must run on the main thread)", Anyone know if it exits a native keras generator to do this, that is, flow images and masks from directories ? or if it is possible to create one in python and import it to R ? it is very frustating to use only 1 worker.

Here is the code that works so far : 

```
setwd("E:/segmentation_flow_from_directory/")

library(keras)

set.seed(666)
batch_size <- 16
epochs <- 2 
lr_rate=0.0001

# #path to image folders
train_image_files_path <- "./IMG/" 
train_mask_files_path <- "./MASK/"

# # image size
img_width <- 128
img_height <- 128
target_size <- c(img_width, img_height)

# # RGB = 3 channels
channels <- 3

# # data augmentation

# # image generator
train_data_gen = image_data_generator(
  rescale = 1/255,
  rotation_range = 180,
  horizontal_flip = TRUE,
  vertical_flip = TRUE
)

# # mask generator
train_mask_gen = image_data_generator(
  rescale = 1/255,
  rotation_range = 180,
  horizontal_flip = TRUE,
  vertical_flip = TRUE
)

# # flow image from image directory 
train_image_array_gen <- flow_images_from_directory(train_image_files_path, 
                                                    train_data_gen,
                                                    target_size = target_size,
                                                    class_mode = NULL,
                                                    color_mode = "rgb",
                                                    seed = 42,
                                                   batch_size = batch_size)
# # flow image from mask directory 
train_mask_array_gen <- flow_images_from_directory(train_mask_files_path, 
                                                    train_mask_gen,
                                                    target_size = target_size,
                                                    class_mode = NULL,
                                                    color_mode = "grayscale",
                                                    seed = 42,
                                                   batch_size = batch_size)

# # combine the two iterators 
train_iterator <- function() {
  x1 <- iter_next(train_image_array_gen)
  x2 <- iter_next(train_mask_array_gen)
  list (x1, x2)
}

# # number of training samples
train_samples <- train_image_array_gen$n

# # custom metric function
dice_coef <- custom_metric("custom", function(y_true, y_pred, smooth = 1.0) {
  y_true_f <- k_flatten(y_true)
  y_pred_f <- k_flatten(y_pred)
  intersection <- k_sum(y_true_f * y_pred_f)
  result <- (2 * intersection + smooth) / 
    (k_sum(y_true_f) + k_sum(y_pred_f) + smooth)
  return(result)
})

# # loss function
bce_dice_loss <- function(y_true, y_pred) {
  result <- loss_binary_crossentropy(y_true, y_pred) +
    (1 - dice_coef(y_true, y_pred))
  return(result)
}


# # U-net 128 -----------------------------------------------------

get_unet_128 <- function(input_shape = c(128, 128, 3),
                         num_classes = 1) {
  
  inputs <- layer_input(shape = input_shape)
  # # 128
  
  down1 <- inputs %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 64, kernel_size = c(3, 3), padding = "same") %>%
    layer_batch_normalization() %>%
    layer_activation("relu") %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 64, kernel_size = c(3, 3), padding = "same") %>%
    layer_batch_normalization() %>%
    layer_activation("relu") 
  down1_pool <- down1 %>%
    layer_max_pooling_2d(pool_size = c(2, 2), strides = c(2, 2))
  # # 64
  
  down2 <- down1_pool %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 128, kernel_size = c(3, 3), padding = "same") %>%
    layer_batch_normalization() %>%
    layer_activation("relu") %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 128, kernel_size = c(3, 3), padding = "same") %>%
    layer_batch_normalization() %>%
    layer_activation("relu") 
  down2_pool <- down2 %>%
    layer_max_pooling_2d(pool_size = c(2, 2), strides = c(2, 2))
  # # 32
  
  down3 <- down2_pool %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 256, kernel_size = c(3, 3), padding = "same") %>%
    layer_batch_normalization() %>%
    layer_activation("relu") %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 256, kernel_size = c(3, 3), padding = "same") %>%
    layer_batch_normalization() %>%
    layer_activation("relu") 
  down3_pool <- down3 %>%
    layer_max_pooling_2d(pool_size = c(2, 2), strides = c(2, 2))
  # # 16
  
  down4 <- down3_pool %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 512, kernel_size = c(3, 3), padding = "same") %>%
    layer_batch_normalization() %>%
    layer_activation("relu") %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 512, kernel_size = c(3, 3), padding = "same") %>%
    layer_batch_normalization() %>%
    layer_activation("relu") 
  down4_pool <- down4 %>%
    layer_max_pooling_2d(pool_size = c(2, 2), strides = c(2, 2))
  # # 8
  
  center <- down4_pool %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 1024, kernel_size = c(3, 3), padding = "same") %>%
    layer_batch_normalization() %>%
    layer_activation("relu") %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 1024, kernel_size = c(3, 3), padding = "same") %>%
    layer_batch_normalization() %>%
    layer_activation("relu") 
  # # center
  
  up4 <- center %>%
    layer_upsampling_2d(size = c(2, 2)) %>%
    {layer_concatenate(inputs = list(down4, .), axis = 3)} %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 512, kernel_size = c(3, 3), padding = "same") %>%
    layer_batch_normalization() %>%
    layer_activation("relu") %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 512, kernel_size = c(3, 3), padding = "same") %>%
    layer_batch_normalization() %>%
    layer_activation("relu") %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 512, kernel_size = c(3, 3), padding = "same") %>%
    layer_batch_normalization() %>%
    layer_activation("relu")
  # # 16
  
  up3 <- up4 %>%
    layer_upsampling_2d(size = c(2, 2)) %>%
    {layer_concatenate(inputs = list(down3, .), axis = 3)} %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 256, kernel_size = c(3, 3), padding = "same") %>%
    layer_batch_normalization() %>%
    layer_activation("relu") %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 256, kernel_size = c(3, 3), padding = "same") %>%
    layer_batch_normalization() %>%
    layer_activation("relu") %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 256, kernel_size = c(3, 3), padding = "same") %>%
    layer_batch_normalization() %>%
    layer_activation("relu")
  # # 32
  
  up2 <- up3 %>%
    layer_upsampling_2d(size = c(2, 2)) %>%
    {layer_concatenate(inputs = list(down2, .), axis = 3)} %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 128, kernel_size = c(3, 3), padding = "same") %>%
    layer_batch_normalization() %>%
    layer_activation("relu") %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 128, kernel_size = c(3, 3), padding = "same") %>%
    layer_batch_normalization() %>%
    layer_activation("relu") %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 128, kernel_size = c(3, 3), padding = "same") %>%
    layer_batch_normalization() %>%
    layer_activation("relu")
  # # 64
  
  up1 <- up2 %>%
    layer_upsampling_2d(size = c(2, 2)) %>%
    {layer_concatenate(inputs = list(down1, .), axis = 3)} %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 64, kernel_size = c(3, 3), padding = "same") %>%
    layer_batch_normalization() %>%
    layer_activation("relu") %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 64, kernel_size = c(3, 3), padding = "same") %>%
    layer_batch_normalization() %>%
    layer_activation("relu") %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = 64, kernel_size = c(3, 3), padding = "same") %>%
    layer_batch_normalization() %>%
    layer_activation("relu")
  # # 128
  
  classify <- layer_conv_2d(up1,
                            filters = num_classes, 
                            kernel_size = c(1, 1),
                            activation = "sigmoid")
  
  
  model <- keras_model(
    inputs = inputs,
    outputs = classify
  )
  
  model %>% compile(
    optimizer = optimizer_rmsprop(lr = lr_rate),
    loss = bce_dice_loss,
    metrics = c(dice_coef)
  )
  
  return(model)
}

model <- get_unet_128()


# # fit
hist <- model %>% fit_generator(
  # # training data
  train_iterator,
  
  # # epochs
  steps_per_epoch = as.integer(train_samples / batch_size), 
  epochs = epochs, 
 
  # # parallel processor 
  workers=1,
  
  # # print progress
  verbose = 2,
  callbacks = list(
  
  # # save accuracies and losses values
  callback_csv_logger("./epoch_history/epoch_history.csv", separator = ";", append = FALSE),
  
  # # save best model weights
  callback_model_checkpoint("./weights/unet_flow_{epoch:03d}.h5",monitor="custom", save_best_only = TRUE,save_freq = NULL,mode="max")
    
  )
)


```

title: Python to R issue with input shape
description:
Hi, @skeydan @dfalbel.

I try to convert [python](https://keras-team.github.io/keras-tuner/tutorials/subclass-tuner/) to R for kerastuneR but facing an issue. I cannot understand why it throws an error. Below is a reproducible example. The problem is when I try to pass a list of images and respective labels into ```tf$GradientTape()``` it throws: ``` RuntimeError: Evaluation error: argument is of length zero. ```. Could you help with that, please?

```
library(reticulate)
k_tuner = import('kerastuner')
library(keras)
library(tensorflow)
library(dplyr)
library(tfdatasets)

conv_build_model = function(hp) {
  'Builds a convolutional model.'
  inputs = tf$keras$Input(shape=c(28L, 28L, 1L))
  
  x = inputs
  
  for (i in 1:hp$Int('conv_layers', 1L, 3L, default=3L)) {
    x = tf$keras$layers$Conv2D(filters = hp$Int(paste('filters_', i, sep = ''), 4L, 32L, step=4L, default=8L),
                               kernel_size = hp$Int(paste('kernel_size_', i, sep = ''), 3L, 5L),
                               activation ='relu',
                               padding='same')(x)
    if (hp$Choice(paste('pooling', i, sep = ''), c('max', 'avg')) == 'max') {
      x = tf$keras$layers$MaxPooling2D()(x)
    } else {
      x = tf$keras$layers$AveragePooling2D()(x)
    }
    x = tf$keras$layers$BatchNormalization()(x) 
    x =  tf$keras$layers$ReLU()(x)
    
  }
  if (hp$Choice('global_pooling', c('max', 'avg')) == 'max') {
    x =  tf$keras$layers$GlobalMaxPool2D()(x)
  } else {
    x = tf$keras$layers$GlobalAveragePooling2D()(x)
  }
  
  outputs = tf$keras$layers$Dense(10L, activation='softmax')(x)
  model = tf$keras$Model(inputs, outputs)
  optimizer = hp$Choice('optimizer', c('adam', 'sgd'))
  model %>% compile(optimizer, loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy', metrics='accuracy')
  return(model)
}

MyTuner = reticulate::PyClass(
  'Tuner',
  inherit = k_tuner$Tuner,
  list(
    run_trial = function(self, trial, train_ds){
      hp = trial$hyperparameters
      train_ds = train_ds$batch(hp$Int('batch_size', 32L, 128L, step=32L, default=64L))
      model = self$hypermodel$build(trial$hyperparameters)
      lr = hp$Float('learning_rate', 1e-4, 1e-2, sampling='log', default=1e-3)
      optimizer = tf$keras$optimizers$Adam(lr)
      epoch_loss_metric = tf$keras$metrics$Mean()
      
      # problem
      run_train_step = function(data){
        images = data[[1]]
        labels = data[[2]]
        
        with (tf$GradientTape() %as% tape,{
          logits = model(images)
          loss = tf$keras$losses$sparse_categorical_crossentropy(labels, logits)
          if(model$losses){
            loss = loss + tf$math$add_n(model$losses)
          }
          gradients = tape$gradient(loss, model$trainable_variables)
        })
        optimizer$apply_gradients(transpose(list(gradients, model$trainable_variables)))
        epoch_loss_metric$update_state(loss)
        loss
      }
      
      for (epoch in 1:10) {
        print(paste('Epoch',epoch))
        self$on_epoch_begin(trial, model, epoch, logs= list())
        intializer = make_iterator_one_shot(train_ds)
        
        for (batch in 1:length(iterate(train_ds))) {
          
          init_next = iter_next(intializer)
          
          self$on_batch_begin(trial, model, batch, logs=list())
          print('done self$on_batch_begin')
          print(init_next)
          batch_loss = round(run_train_step(init_next),2)
          self$on_batch_end(trial, model, batch, logs=list(paste('loss', batch_loss)))
          
          if (batch %% 100 == 0){
            loss = epoch_loss_metric$result()$numpy()
            print('Batch',batch,  'Average loss', loss)
          }
        }
        
        epoch_loss = epoch_loss_metric$result()$numpy()
        self$on_epoch_end(trial, model, epoch, logs=list(paste('loss', epoch_loss)))
        epoch_loss_metric$reset_states()
      }
    }
  )
)


main = function(){
  tuner = MyTuner(
    oracle=k_tuner$oracles$BayesianOptimization(
      objective=k_tuner$Objective('loss', 'min'),
      max_trials=1L),
    hypermodel=conv_build_model,
    directory='results',

title: Installation w/ Miniconda, Reticulate 1.14, Tensorflow 2.0.0 & Keras 2.2.5.0 failing
description:
In connection with the new version of [reticulate v1.14](https://blog.rstudio.com/2019/12/20/reticulate-1-14/) and after quite a few problems to get [Keras available](https://community.rstudio.com/t/reticulate-1-14-together-with-miniconda3-and-tensorflow-not-working/49180), I encountered a rather serious problem. In an existing program written under `keras v2.2.0.9000`, `reticulate v1.10` and `tensorflow v1.9` and since then run successfully many times, the command 
```
model %>% compile(
  optimizer = "adam",
  loss = list(loss_mean_squared_error, loss_categorical_crossentropy)
)
```
now run under `reticulate 1.14`, `tensorflow 2.0.0` and `keras 2.2.5.0`, produce the following error message:

> error in UseMethod ("compile") : 
> not applicable method 'compile' applied for object of class "c('keras._impl.keras.engine.training.Model', 'keras._impl.keras.engine.topology.Network', 'tensorflow.python.layers.network.GraphNetwork', 'keras._impl.keras.engine.topology.Layer', 'tensorflow.python.layers.base.Layer', 'python.builtin.object')" 

Similarly, the command
```
model %>% fit(x = x,
              y = list(y1, y2),
              sample_weight = list(sample_weights, sample_weights),
              epochs = 10)
```
produces the error message

> error in UseMethod ("fit") : 
> not applicable method 'compile' applied for object of class  "c('keras._impl.keras.engine.training.Model', 'keras._impl.keras.engine.topology.Network', 'tensorflow.python.layers.network.GraphNetwork', 'keras._impl.keras.engine.topology.Layer', 'tensorflow.python.layers.base.Layer', 'python.builtin.object')" 

So - which method would then be applicable for compilation? Consulting the `keras 2.2.5.0` index w.r.t. command `compile` shows that `compile` as such doesn't exist as entry in the index any more, but only

> `compile.keras.engine.training.Model` ... Configure a Keras model for training

However, under this symbolic headline I find the same description as earlier under keyword `compile(...)` and I cannnot detect anything wrong within the command used as above. Correspondingly the situation for `fit()`.

Moreover, the function `to_categorical(y, num_classes = NULL, ...)` now seems to require specification of `num_classes` explicitely, since without this specification (as it was used up to now), a mysterious error message

> Error: Keras loaded from tensorflow v1.5, however version 1.9 is required. Please update with tensorflow::install_tensorflow()

appears. And, really, the command `tensorflow::tf_config()` shows, much to my surprise,

> TensorFlow v1.5.0 (C:\...\Local\conda\conda\envs\R-TENS~1\lib\site-packages\tensorflow\__init__.p)
> Python v3.6 (C:/.../Local/conda/conda/envs/r-tensorflow/python.exe)

Note that in my case actually `tensorflow v2.0.0` has been installed; the recommended command to install `tensorflow v1.9` (sic!) at this point sounds like a dire reminiscence to my (lost) previous era with Keras. And there is no way back: an attempt to reinstall `tensorflow 1.9` automatically leads to reinstallation of `tensorflow 2.0.0`, since `tensorflow 1.9` is not available for `R 3.6.2`. Catch 362, so to speak...

I am really at a loss how to proceed. Any useful hint would be highly appreciated.

Tnx in advance,
Leo Faltin

title: Fix to clear GPU memory TF 2.0
description:
I thought this would be useful for anyone tearing their hair out like me yesterday.

I had to generate hundreds of models for a model selection project, and I found that the GPU RAM gets eaten up pretty quickly as the previous models don't get removed from the GPU ram.

I have cobbled together some scripts (credit to this page "https://forums.fast.ai/t/tip-clear-tensorflow-gpu-memory/1979/7") to produce a function which works with tensorflow 2.0 to clear the gpu. I have tested on my machine (windows 10, python 3.7, conda tf2.0, nvidia quadro p4000). This clears the python tf session from within the R_session, releasing the GPU RAM. The function can be placed within a loop in rstudio, saving the need to run an external bash script. 

`
library(reticulate)
py_run_string("from keras import backend as K")
py_run_string("from keras.backend.tensorflow_backend import set_session;")
py_run_string("from keras.backend.tensorflow_backend import clear_session;")
py_run_string("from keras.backend.tensorflow_backend import get_session;")

clear_gpu <- function(){
py_run_string("cfg = K.config_pb2.ConfigProto()")
py_run_string("cfg.gpu_options.allow_growth = True")
py_run_string("K.set_session(K.tf.compat.v1.Session(config=cfg))")
k_clear_session()
}

#now clear with this command
clear_gpu()
`
