title: R/Keras webpage example code fails due to undocumented requirement
description:
I'm currently unable to successfully run the MNIST example from the R/Keras [webpage](https://keras.rstudio.com/).  Despite the installation apparently completing successfully, the example code fails at the first hurdle:
```
> mnist <- dataset_mnist()
Error: Installation of Python not found, Python bindings not loaded.
```
On investigation, this appears to be because the package assumes Python will be installed on my system*.  Said system is a corporate laptop with very restrictive IT policies**, which means that I am unable to install Python (or more generally Conda).  As such, it appears that I will never be able to get Keras to run in its current form.

That's certainly not the RStudio team's fault - I'm grateful for your efforts, and you're not responsible for my company's IT policies.  However, it would have been helpful to know this prerequisite up-front before I got all enthusiastic :)

Unless there's a way of working round this restriction, you may want to add text to the R/Keras webpage, for example in the form of a Requirements subsection of the Getting Started section, making clear that Python and/or Conda is necessary for this package to function.

\* Laptop is running Windows 10 Enterprise, RStudio 1.1.383, and R 3.4.3 (2017-11-30).

\** All permissions are applied at the organisation level (i.e. outside my control) on a per-application basis.  So RStudio can run devtools::install_github because the system sees it as an extension of its existing package management permissions, but I can't install Python myself.  If there is any way to install Python via devtools then that would fix the problem, but some experimentation suggests that this isn't possible (which makes sense really).

title: embedding layer with LSTM autoencoder
description:
Hello, 

I have found the following answer but I want to make sure it really does not have any other option:

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/44731059/keras-lstm-autoencoder-with-embedding-layer

The following use of embedding layer with timeseries works:

```
num_features = 4
nb_classes =3
num_steps =10


X <- matrix(0,nrow=128,ncol=num_features)

model %>%
layer_embedding(num_features, num_steps) %>%
layer_lstm(units = num_features, return_sequences=FALSE) %>% 
layer_dense(units=nb_classes, activation='linear')

title: Apply weights to several masks for training U-Net on segmentation task
description:
Dear all,

I am working on a segmentation task. My encoder-decoder of choice is U-Net. My aim is to use as ground-truth one mask defining the object itself and one mask defining the border of the object. I am using this approach as it was outperforming other methodologies for instance at the Data Science Bowl 2018.
Some of the problems I had with the architecture of the U-Net were solved here: 
https://github.com/rstudio/keras/issues/511

The input of my model is:
input_1 (InputLayer)                    (None, 512, 512, 1)                                       

The output of my model is:
conv2d_15 (Conv2D)                      (None, 512, 512, 2)

The initial results looks good except at the boundaries between objects. It seems that this is a recurrent problem in semantic segmentation using U-Net. As far as I understand it is a class imbalance problem. As the borders of the objects covers a much lower fraction of the image than the mask of the object itself, the model emphasizes what is "sees" the most. Therefore adding weights to the two masks would help to "tell" the model where to focus. In my case I would like to assign for example 0.2 weight to the mask of the object itself and 0.8 weight to the border mask respectively. However I couldn't figure out how to apply this concretely to my model. 

I assumed that with sample_weight or class_weight it would work. However I didn't manage to apply the weights with those two parameters. 

Just to give all the details here is the loss function I am currently using:
`dice_coef <- function(y_true, y_pred, smooth = 1.0){
  y_true_f <- k_flatten(y_true)
  y_pred_f <- k_flatten(y_pred)
  intersection <- k_sum(y_true_f * y_pred_f)
  #(2 * intersection + smooth) / (k_sum(y_true_f) + k_sum(y_pred_f) + smooth) 
  k_mean((2 * intersection + smooth) / (k_sum(y_true_f) + k_sum(y_pred_f) + smooth)) # for use in combination with bce
}
attr(dice_coef, "py_function_name") <- "dice_coef"`
`dice_coef_loss_for_bce <- function(y_true, y_pred){
  1 - dice_coef(y_true, y_pred)
}
attr(dice_coef_loss_for_bce, "py_function_name") <- "dice_coef_loss_for_bce"`
`dice_coef_loss_bce <- function(y_true, y_pred, dice = 0.5, bce = 0.5){
  loss_binary_crossentropy(y_true, y_pred) * bce + dice_coef_loss_for_bce(y_true, y_pred) * dice
}
attr(dice_coef_loss_bce, "py_function_name") <- "dice_coef_loss_bce"`


When I tried to apply loss_weights when I compiled the model:
`model <- model %>%
    compile(loss = dice_coef_loss_bce, 
            optimizer = 'adam',
            metrics = c(dice_coef),
            loss_weights = list(0.2, 0.8)
            )`
I got this error
`Error in py_call_impl(callable, dots$args, dots$keywords) : 
  ValueError: When passing a list as loss_weights, it should have one entry per model output.
  The model has 1 outputs, but you passed loss_weights=[0.2, 0.8]`

I also tried sample_weight (as it seems that class weight doesn't handle objects with more than 2D).
`history <- model %>%
    fit(X,
        Y,
        batch_size = BATCH_SIZE,
        epochs = EPOCHS,
        validation_split = 0.2,
        verbose = 1,
        callbacks = list(early_stopping),
        class_weight = list("1" = 0.2, "2" = 0.8)
        )
`
This is the error I get.		
`Error in py_call_impl(callable, dots$args, dots$keywords) : 
  ValueError: `class_weight` not supported for 3+ dimensional targets.`

Now with sample_weight:
`history <- model %>%
    fit(X,
        Y,
        batch_size = BATCH_SIZE,
        epochs = EPOCHS,
        validation_split = 0.2,
        verbose = 1,
        callbacks = list(early_stopping),
        sample_weight = dict(list("1" = 0.2, "2" = 0.8))
        )`
The corresponding error:	
`Error in dim(x) <- length(x) : invalid first argument`

My question is simple, how can I apply the weights to my two masks so that the U-Net is getting trained properly? I am currently thinking that there must be an issue with the architecture of the U-Net but can't point exactly at where it is.

Many thanks in advance for your help.

Best wishes,

Mathieu

    import tensorflow as tf

			bias_regularizer = regularizer_l1(FLAGS$regularizer_rate)
		)) %>%
		bidirectional(layer_lstm(
			units = FLAGS$layer_8, 
			return_sequences = TRUE, 
			bias_regularizer = regularizer_l1(FLAGS$regularizer_rate)
		)) %>%
		layer_spatial_dropout_1d(rate = FLAGS$dropout_rate_2) %>%
		layer_batch_normalization() %>%
		layer_flatten() %>%
		layer_dense(length(input_chars)) %>%
		layer_activation(FLAGS$activation)
		
blstm %>% compile(
    loss = FLAGS$loss,
    optimizer = optimizer_nadam(lr = FLAGS$learning_rate),
    metrics = FLAGS$metrics
)

blstm %>% fit(
	x_train, y_train,
	batch_size = FLAGS$batch_size,
	epochs = FLAGS$epochs,
	validation_split = 0.2,
	verbose = 1,
	view_metrics = TRUE,
	callbacks = c(
		callback_model_checkpoint('blstm.h5'), 
		callback_early_stopping(
			monitor = FLAGS$monitor, 
			patience = FLAGS$patience, 
			min_delta = FLAGS$min_delta))
)

```
I'm not sure what's going on? That's a fairly generic Python error I believe, usually due to passing the wrong input class to a function. Is perhaps the entire Flags function being passed?

Strangely enough, if I do change the `fit()` to use one of the `FLAGS `in callback, it requires a full system restart. No amount of `k_clear_session()` or changing the backend, terminating the R environment and restarting it, etc, seems to fix it. Is keras instantiating a python instance? Could we get a way to restart that python instance if that is the case?

EDIT: On further diagnosis, it seems the type values of each `FLAGS` is correct, however the system is giving me inconsistent results. The `fit()` function seems to generate an error sometimes if I even use `FLAGS$batch_size`, even through a system restart. That's very perplexing. Any ideas?

title: adaptive loss or class weights
description:
When treating instationary, albeit statistically slowly changing data and the network is learning faster than the data is changing, it would be interesting to adapt the network on the fly as these changes occur. Just imagine the case that in a classification task the relative proportion of the classes changes; or in the case of an inception network the contributions of/to the various channels might change and concatenation of these channels should be adapted accordingly in order to keep the network optimized.

My question is: How would it be possible to achieve this aim?

From Keras documentation I cannot find out when exactly the parameters class_weight (for multiple class problems) and loss_weight (for multiple output problems) are read by the program and applied to the network. 

1. Are they only read at compilation?  
2. Are they read between single fit()-cycles, i.e. after a preprogrammed number of epochs?
3. Are they read between single epochs of one particular fit()-cycle?

Obviously, case 3. would be the one providing a maximum of programming freedom. In contrast to that, case 1. would require new compilation, which probably means that network parameters learned until then will be lost. 

Case 2. could potentially indicate a solution - if the commands save/load_model_weights_hdf5 really concern _only_ the network layers and not loss/class_weights: one could then save the newly learned model layers, load a new list of class/loss_weights (e.g. by compilation - or how else?), and then reload the model_weights. Again, the documentation does not provide any hint to that approach.

Any pertinent comment would be welcome - thanks in advance!
Leo

iou_thresholds = np.array([0.5, 0.55, 0.6, 0.65, 0.7, 0.75, 0.8, 0.85, 0.9, 0.95])

def iou(img_true, img_pred):
    i = np.sum((img_true*img_pred) >0)
    u = np.sum((img_true + img_pred) >0)
    if u == 0:
        return u
    return i/u

def iou_metric(imgs_true, imgs_pred):
    num_images = len(imgs_true)

description:

     $ Total.Sum: num  0.0159 0.0233 0.0234 0.024 0.0157 ...
     $ weekday  : num  0.25 0.5 0.75 1 0 0.25 0.5 0.75 1 0 ...

I have 256 training examples. 
Pre-processing the data for the model - 
    
    # Splitting into training and testing set

    model %>% 
      layer_gru(units = 32, batch_input_shape = c(256, 2, 1), return_sequences = T, stateful = T, activation = "relu") %>%

title: Using a trained neural network in a custom loss function in keras
description:
Hi,

Here's what I want to do: I want to train an autoencoder for a toy example, let's say MNIST. In particular, I want my loss function to be a linear combination of MSE and the Euclidean distance of the original image and the reconstructed image in a feature space. 

Loss = MSE + ||F(x) - F(x')||^2

Here, the F function I am looking for, is itself an other neural network.

This is what I have done so far:

`K <- backend()


mnist <- dataset_mnist()
x_train <- mnist$train$x
y_train <- mnist$train$y
x_test <- mnist$test$x
y_test <- mnist$test$y
x_train <- array_reshape(x_train, c(nrow(x_train), 784))
x_test <- array_reshape(x_test, c(nrow(x_test), 784))

x_train <- x_train / 255
x_test <- x_test / 255
y_train <- to_categorical(y_train, 10)
y_test <- to_categorical(y_test, 10)


opt = optimizer_adamax(lr = 0.002)

inputs <- layer_input(shape = shape(784), name = "input_t")
hidden_layers <- inputs %>%
  layer_dense(units = 256 , activation = "selu") %>%
  layer_dropout(0.3) %>%
  layer_dense(units = 128 , activation = "selu") %>%
  layer_dropout(0.3) %>%
  layer_dense(units = 16 , activation = "selu", name = "encoded")


decoder<- hidden_layers %>%
  layer_dropout(0.4) %>% 
  layer_dense(units = 10 , activation = "softmax")

model <- keras_model(inputs = inputs, outputs = decoder)



model %>%
  compile(
    loss = 'categorical_crossentropy',
    optimizer = opt , metrics = "acc")


summary(model)


history <- model %>% fit(
  x_train, y_train, 
  epochs = 30, batch_size = 128, 
  validation_split = 0.2
)

f = K$Function(list(model$layers[[1]]$input),
               list(model$layers[[7]]$output))`

Here f is the F(.) I had in the loss function.

Here is the definition of the autoencoder:

`opt = optimizer_adamax(lr = 0.002)

ae_inputs <- layer_input(shape = shape(784), name = "input_t")
encoder <- ae_inputs %>%
  layer_dense(units = 256 , activation = "selu") %>%
  layer_dropout(0.3) %>%
  layer_dense(units = 64 , activation = "selu") %>%
  layer_dropout(0.3) %>%
  layer_dense(units = 32 , activation = "selu", name = "encoded")


decoder<- encoder %>%
  layer_dense(units = 128 , activation = "selu") %>%
  layer_dropout(0.3) %>%
  layer_dense(units = 256 , activation = "selu") %>%
  layer_dropout(0.1) %>%
  layer_dense(units = 512 , activation = "selu") %>% 
  layer_dense(units = 784 , activation = "sigmoid")

ae <- keras_model(inputs = ae_inputs, outputs = decoder)



ae %>%
  compile(
    loss = custom_loss,
    optimizer = opt , metrics = "mae")`
and here is the loss function:

`
custom_loss <- function(y_true, y_pred) {
  mse = K$mean(K$square(y_true - y_pred))
  pred_feature_map = f(list(K$eval(y_pred)))
  true_feature_map = f(list(K$eval(y_true)))
  similarity =  K$mean(K$square( pred_feature_map - pred_feature_map ))
  loss = similarity + mse
return(loss)
}
`

Unfortunately, I get an error which I dont know how to handle it...

Error in py_call_impl(callable, dots$args, dots$keywords) :

I would appreciate if anyone could help me regarding this matter. 

Many thanks...

title: Error in do.call(object$evaluate, args) :    'what' must be a function or character string
description:
Hi all,
I have been training my model on my AWS instance for 5 days. Now, when the time finally came to see how it does with unseen data, I tried passing
```
model%>%
  evaluate(list(x1, x2), y)

and

model%>%
  predict_classes(list(x1, x2))
```

I tried passing `keras:::evaluate()` instead, thinking there might be another `evaluate()` function among the loaded packages, but got the same result.
I also ran `update.packages()` and `install_keras()` again, just in case. No change.

Does anyone know what may be going on here?

title: ValueError: The output of the "schedule" function should be float
description:
Below is some code, which is throwing an error.  The problem with this is that R does not have a `float()` function, so I am not sure why the error is happening.

    eps <- 1000
    
    
    spikes_model <- function(maxiter, total_spikes = 10, max_height = 0.001, min_height = 0.000005, decay_rate = 0.2) {
      value_at_iteration <- rep(0, maxiter)
      spike_at <- maxiter / total_spikes
      current_rate <- min_height
      holder_timeval <- 0
      for(i in 1:maxiter) {
        spike_indicator <- i / spike_at
        if (is.wholenumber(spike_indicator)) {
          current_rate <- max_height
          value_at_iteration[i] <- current_rate
          holder_timeval <- spike_indicator
        } else if (i < spike_at) {
          current_rate <- min_height
          value_at_iteration[i] <- current_rate
        } else {
          timeval <- i - (holder_timeval*spike_at)
          current_rate <- max_height*exp(-decay_rate*timeval) + min_height
          value_at_iteration[i] <- current_rate
        }
      }
      return(value_at_iteration)
    }
    
    sch <- spikes_model(eps)
    
    lr_schedule <- function(epoch, lr) {
      lrn <- sch[epoch]
      lrn <- as.numeric(lrn)
      return(lrn)
    }
    
    # # plot learning rate evolution
    # ln <- NULL
    # for (i in 1:eps) {
    #   blah <- lr_schedule(i)
    #   ln[i] <- blah
    # }
    # plot(ln, type="l")

      x=X.train, y=Y.train,
      epochs=eps, batch_size=nrow(X.train),

<weibull_loglik_discrete = function(y_true, y_pred) {
  K = backend()
  y_true = k_reshape(y_true, c(1024, 2))
  y_pred = k_reshape(y_pred, c(1024, 2))
 
  y_ = y_true[, 1]
  u_ = y_true[, 2]
  a_ = y_pred[, 1]
  b_ = y_pred[, 2]

  hazard0 = ((y_ + 1e-35) / a_) ^ b_
  hazard1 = ((y_ + 1) / a_) ^ b_

  return(-1 * k_mean(u_ * k_log(k_exp(hazard1 - hazard0) - 1.0) - hazard1))
}

weibull_activate = function(ab) {
  a = k_exp(ab[, 1])
  b = k_softplus(ab[, 2])
  
  a = k_reshape(a, c(length(a), 1))

title: Summarizing multiple training histories
description:
Hi, I'm working on a problem where I have a large collection of
related training history data, and I'm wondering if there are any
keras/R tools to help summarize and/or view that combined history.
I'm not looking to simply generate a grid of n related but independent
graphs from plot.keras_training_history().  Rather, I'm looking for
something more general to help me understand what the "typical"
training history was across a set of related models.

The context is a backtest that predicts a time series.  For a
straightforward backtest example, see this article:

  https://blogs.rstudio.com/tensorflow/posts/2018-06-25-sunspots-lstm/

As in the sunspot example, I have a series of models generated on
sliding windows that expose more and more of the underlying data over
time.  This kind of thing crops up in many time series contexts.  The
common element: each rollforward window generates a "freshly trained"
model, with its own training history, but all the models are related
in having the same architecture and in addressing the same problem.
This same issue can also happen cross sectionally, when you train
separate models for various problems that share some common element.

The key is that the a "good" approach to training the architecture
should measure out as good on "most" of the models, but likely not on
all of them.  You would not want to tune your training hyperparameters
while looking at just one model, you instead want a feel for typical
training history, outliers, etc.

My first thought was to take the various metric histories and compute
summary info, such as the mean loss across all models at epoch 1, 2,
3, etc, percentiles, etc, and then display a graph or table of those
combined metrics.  But there are many issues that glosses over (is
some "history normalization" appropriate, how to handle NAs due to
early stopping in some models, etc)

Can you offer any pointers to tools or research touching on these
multi-model issues, or perhaps advice on alternative ways to think
about them?

Thanks.

title: Clarification on effect of time_distributed in keras
description:
Most blog posts on time series multi-step-ahead prediction with Keras (using R or Python) use `time_distributed`to connect the sequence output from the last RNN layer to the `dense` output (cf. the often cited 
https://machinelearningmastery.com/timedistributed-layer-for-long-short-term-memory-networks-in-python/
).

There is confusion about the purpose of using  `time_distributed(layer_dense(...))` instead of `layer_dense(...)` only. Evidently with Keras > 2.0, there is no difference between both versions (cf. 
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/47305618/what-is-the-role-of-timedistributed-layer-in-keras 
and e.g.  
https://github.com/keras-team/keras/issues/278
).

Just to be "empirically convinced", here are 2 tests on synthetic data that show that:
1) the structure of the models (parameters) is the same in both cases, and
2) loss is very nearly the same for both versions.

We separately test for the frequent use case where we're predicting a single series (example 1) and for predicting  two series at the same time (example 2). We're trying to reduce random effects by setting a seed and initializing the weights to 0 (something you would not want to do in real life).
We're looping over different sizes of the timesteps dimension and clearly see the above points confirmed.

Aside: The weight matrices themselves are not identical and may even be very different - just to achieve the same result - as we're still not eliminating all sources of random (`time_distributed` uses an RNN cell internally on whose initialization we can't exert any influence).

Example 1

```
library(keras)

n_tsteps <- 3:10
  
batch_size <- 10
n_epochs <- 200

data <- rep(1:7, 10) + rnorm(70) %>% round(digits = 2)

for (t in seq_along(n_tsteps)) {
  print(n_tsteps[t])
  
  data_matrix <-
    sapply(1:(length(data) - n_tsteps[t] * 2 + 1), function(index) {
      data[index:(index + n_tsteps[t] * 2 - 1)]
    }) %>% t()
  data_matrix
  x <- data_matrix[, 1:n_tsteps[t]]
  y <- data_matrix[, (n_tsteps[t] + 1):ncol(data_matrix)]
  dim(x) <- c(dim(x)[1], dim(x)[2], 1)
  dim(y) <- c(dim(y)[1], dim(y)[2], 1)
  
  
  set.seed(7777)
  model1 <- keras_model_sequential()
  model1 %>% time_distributed(layer_dense(units = 1, kernel_initializer = initializer_zeros(), input_shape = c(n_tsteps[t], 1)))
  model1 %>% compile(loss = "mse", optimizer = "adam")
  history <-
    model1 %>% fit(x,
                   y,
                   epochs = n_epochs,
                   batch_size = batch_size,
                   verbose = 0)
  plot(history)
  model1 %>% print()
  model1$get_weights()  %>% print()
  model1 %>% evaluate(x, y) %>% print()
  
  set.seed(7777)
  model2 <- keras_model_sequential()
  model2 %>% layer_dense(units = 1, input_shape = c(n_tsteps[t], 1), kernel_initializer = initializer_zeros())
  model2 %>% print()
  model2 %>% compile(loss = "mse", optimizer = "adam")
  history <-
    model2 %>% fit(x,
                   y,
                   epochs = n_epochs,
                   batch_size = batch_size,
                   verbose = 0)
  plot(history)
  model2$get_weights()  %>%  print()
  model2 %>% evaluate(x, y) %>% print()
  
}
```
Example 2:

```
library(keras)

n_tsteps <- 3:10

n_features <- 2
batch_size <- 10
n_epochs <- 200

col1 <- rep(1:7, 10) + rnorm(70) %>% round(digits = 2)
col2 <- rep(1:70) + rnorm(70) %>% round(digits = 2)

for (t in seq_along(n_tsteps)) {
  print(n_tsteps[t])
  
  col1_matrix <-
    sapply(1:(length(col1) - n_tsteps[t] * 2 + 1), function(index) {
      col1[index:(index + n_tsteps[t] * 2 - 1)]
    }) %>% t()
  col1_matrix
  
  col2_matrix <-
    sapply(1:(length(col2) - n_tsteps[t] * 2 + 1), function(index) {
      col2[index:(index + n_tsteps[t] * 2 - 1)]
    }) %>% t()
  col2_matrix
  
  data_array <-
    array(0, dim = c(nrow(col1_matrix), n_tsteps[t] * 2, n_features))
  data_array[, , 1] <- col1_matrix
  data_array[, , 2] <- col2_matrix
  
  x <- data_array[, 1:n_tsteps[t],]
  y <- data_array[, (n_tsteps[t] + 1):ncol(data_array),]
  
  set.seed(7777)
  model1 <- keras_model_sequential()
  model1 %>% time_distributed(layer_dense(units = n_features,
                                          kernel_initializer = initializer_zeros()),
                              input_shape = c(n_tsteps[t], n_features))
  model1 %>% print()
  model1 %>% compile(loss = "mse", optimizer = "adam")
  history <-
    model1 %>% fit(x,
                   y,
                   epochs = n_epochs,
                   batch_size = batch_size,
                   verbose = 0)
  plot(history)
  model1$get_weights()  %>%  print()
  model1 %>% evaluate(x, y) %>% print()
 
  set.seed(7777)
  model2 <- keras_model_sequential()
  model2 %>% layer_dense(units = n_features,
                         input_shape = c(n_tsteps[t], n_features),
                         kernel_initializer = initializer_zeros())
  model2 %>% print()
  model2 %>% compile(loss = "mse", optimizer = "adam")
  history <-
    model2 %>% fit(x,
                   y,
                   epochs = n_epochs,
                   batch_size = batch_size,
                   verbose = 0)
  plot(history)
  model2$get_weights()  %>%  print()
  model2 %>% evaluate(x, y) %>% print()
}
```

title: Implementing warm restarts using callback_learning_rate_scheduler
description:
I am trying to add my own much much less sofitsticated version of Stochastic Gradient Descent with Warm Restarts, by Loshchilov and Hutter (https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.03983) to my sequence predictor CNN model. The idea is to have the learning rate start at 0.3 and decrease by half at each epoch. Then, at every 15th epoch it would go back to 0.3.
```
LR<-0.3
lr_schedule<-function(epoch) {
      LR/(2 ^ (epoch%%15))
  }
cb_lr<-callback_learning_rate_scheduler(lr_schedule)

model%>%
  compile(loss = 'binary_crossentropy',
          optimizer = 'adam',metrics = c('accuracy'))
history<-model%>%
  fit(x=list(x1,x2,x3),
      y=y,epochs = 31,callbacks=c(cb_lr))
```
The problem is I keep getting the error below, even before the first epoch gets going. Why does it not accept the `lr = ` argument?

title: Feature causes non-convergence
description:
Hi folks,

I want to predict the outcome of a esports game (LOL) but one feature **Gold at minute 15**  causes the model not to converge. Interestingly, the same set of features works with other machine learning libraries (h2o) very well. 

The data looks as follows:

```
library(keras)
library(dplyr)
dat <- get(load(url("https://www.dropbox.com/s/boycb7h8pqvpn83/example_data.Rdata?dl=1")))
glimpse(dat)
# Observations: 6887 
# Variables: 7
# $ blue_win       <dbl> 1, 1, 1, 1, 1
# $ blue_gold_15   <dbl> 23.641, 24.707, 22.736, 24.531, 23.130
# $ red_gold_15    <dbl> 22.592, 24.945, 22.658, 21.969, 22.894
# $ blue_kills_15  <int> 3, 3, 0, 3, 1
# $ red_kills_15   <int> 1, 3, 0, 1, 2
# $ blue_towers_15 <int> 1, 1, 1, 2, 1
# $ red_towers_15  <int> 0, 5, 1, 0, 0
```

A minimal example of a very simple model:

```
fit1 <- keras_model_sequential() %>% 
  layer_dense(units=1, activation = 'sigmoid', input_shape = c(6)) %>% 
  compile(
    loss = "binary_crossentropy",
    optimizer = "adam",
    metrics = "accuracy"
  )

summary(fit1)

fit1 %>% 
  keras::fit(
    x = as.matrix(dat[,-1]), 
    y = matrix(dat[,1], ncol = 1),
    batch_size = 3,
    epochs = 2, 
    validation_split = .2
  )

# Train on 6887 samples, validate on 1722 samples
# Epoch 1/2
# 6887/6887 [==============================] - 4s 598us/step - loss: 6.2859 - acc: 0.0939 - val_loss: 7.4805 - val_acc: 0.0000e+00
# Epoch 2/2
# 6887/6887 [==============================] - 3s 490us/step - loss: 7.2455 - acc: 0.0000e+00 - val_loss: 7.4805 - val_acc: 0.0000e+00
```

What I tried so far:

* not included gold: works perfectly >70% ACC
* different transformations for gold (range01, scale): no difference
* other libraries learn very well from gold

As I am running out of ideas it would be great if someone could give me advice. Thanks in advance!

title: Define a new loss function in Keras (R environment)
description:
Dear all,

Recently, I noticed the quantile regression in Keras (Python), which applies a quantile regression loss function as bellow.

```
import keras.backend as K
def tilted_loss(q,y,f):
    e = (y-f)
    return K.mean(K.maximum(q*e, (q-1)*e), axis=-1)

quantile = 0.5
model.compile(loss=lambda y,f: tilted_loss(quantile,y,f), optimizer='adagrad')
```

I wonder whether I can define this kind of loss function in R when using Keras?
Many thanks for your suggestions in advance.

Best regards,
Songchao

title: compile() drops metric names
description:
`compile()` doesn't pass through a dictionary of metrics, and therefor doesn't allow for matching metrics to a specific named layer. 

Specifically, the names are dropped here https://github.com/rstudio/keras/blob/master/R/model.R#L278

here is a minimal example demonstrating the issue:
``` r
library(keras)

input <- layer_input(10)

core <- input %>% layer_dense(10)

output1 <- core %>% layer_dense(10, name = "output1")
output2 <- core %>% layer_dense(10, name = "output2")
output3 <- core %>% layer_dense(10, name = "output3")

model <- keras_model(input, list(
  output1 = output1,
  output2 = output2,
  output3 = output3
))

model %>% compile(
  "rmsprop", loss = 'mse', 
  metrics = list(
    output1 = 'accuracy',
    output2 = 'mse',
    output3 = 'mae'
  ) 
)

title: Error in py_call_impl(callable, dots$args, dots$keywords) ||| R/Keras
description:
Dear all,
I am trying to run an R script for neural style transfer which I managed to run on a Windows 10 machine. however now that I am trying to this on a linux machine (ubuntu) I am having the same error that i cannot fix despite testing all the solution out there (even reinstalling R and Rstudio).

Here is the error:
```
Error in py_call_impl(callable, dots$args, dots$keywords) : 
  Exception: URL fetch failure on https://github.com/fchollet/deep-learning-models/releases/download/v0.1/vgg16_weights_tf_dim_ordering_tf_kernels_notop.h5: None -- unknown url type: https 
```
It happens when i am trying to load the model:
```
model <- application_vgg16(input_tensor = input_tensor, weights = "imagenet", 
                           include_top = FALSE)
```

Here is the script I used:
```
#' Neural style transfer with Keras.
#' 
#' It is preferable to run this script on a GPU, for speed.
#' 
#' Example result: https://twitter.com/fchollet/status/686631033085677568
#' 
#' Style transfer consists in generating an image
#' with the same "content" as a base image, but with the
#' "style" of a different picture (typically artistic). 
#' 
#' This is achieved through the optimization of a loss function
#' that has 3 components: "style loss", "content loss",
#' and "total variation loss":
#' 
#'  - The total variation loss imposes local spatial continuity between
#'    the pixels of the combination image, giving it visual coherence.
#' 
#'  - The style loss is where the deep learning keeps in --that one is defined
#'    using a deep convolutional neural network. Precisely, it consists in a sum of
#'    L2 distances between the Gram matrices of the representations of
#'    the base image and the style reference image, extracted from
#'    different layers of a convnet (trained on ImageNet). The general idea
#'    is to capture color/texture information at different spatial
#'    scales (fairly large scales --defined by the depth of the layer considered).
#' 
#'  - The content loss is a L2 distance between the features of the base
#'    image (extracted from a deep layer) and the features of the combination image,
#'    keeping the generated image close enough to the original one.
#'
# install.packages("keras")
# install.packages("R6")
# install.packages("purrr")
# install.packages("devtools")
# library(devtools)
# devtools::install_github("rstudio/reticulate", force = T)

library(tidyr)
#library(devtools)
#devtools::install_github("rstudio/keras", force = T)
library(keras)
#install.packages("keras")
#install_keras()
#library(tensorflow)
## try http:// if https:// URLs are not supported
#source("https://bioconductor.org/biocLite.R")
#biocLite()
# biocLite("EBImage")
#?install_tensorflow
#install_tensorflow(GPU = TRUE) # for testing
library(R6)
library(purrr)
library(EBImage)

# Parameters --------------------------------------------------------------
base_dir <- "/home/mydir"
base_image_path <- paste0(base_dir,"/","ToTransform3.jpg")
style_reference_image_path <- paste0(base_dir,"/","Hundertwasser1.jpg")
# display(readImage(base_image_path), method = "raster")
# display(readImage(style_reference_image_path), method= "raster")
iterations <- 100 #increase range 1:1000

# these are the weights of the different loss components
total_variation_weight <- 1
style_weight <- 1
content_weight <- 0.001

# dimensions of the generated picture.
img <- image_load(base_image_path)
width <- img$size[[1]]
height <- img$size[[2]]
img_nrows <- 400
img_ncols <- as.integer(width * img_nrows / height)

# Functions ---------------------------------------------------------------

# util function to open, resize and format pictures into appropriate tensors
preprocess_image <- function(path){
  img <- image_load(path, target_size = c(img_nrows, img_ncols)) %>%
    image_to_array() %>%
    array_reshape(c(1, dim(.)))
  imagenet_preprocess_input(img)
}

# util function to convert a tensor into a valid image
# also turn BGR into RGB.
deprocess_image <- function(x){
  x <- x[1,,,]
  # Remove zero-center by mean pixel
  x[,,1] <- x[,,1] + 103.939
  x[,,2] <- x[,,2] + 116.779
  x[,,3] <- x[,,3] + 123.68
  # BGR -> RGB
  x <- x[,,c(3,2,1)]
  # clip to interval 0, 255
  x[x > 255] <- 255
  x[x < 0] <- 0
  x[] <- as.integer(x)/255
  x
}

# Defining the model ------------------------------------------------------

# get tensor representations of our images
base_image <- k_variable(preprocess_image(base_image_path))
style_reference_image <- k_variable(preprocess_image(style_reference_image_path))

# this will contain our generated image
combination_image <- k_placeholder(c(1, img_nrows, img_ncols, 3))

# combine the 3 images into a single Keras tensor
input_tensor <- k_concatenate(list(base_image, style_reference_image, 
                                   combination_image), axis = 1)

# build the VGG16 network with our 3 images as input
# the model will be loaded with pre-trained ImageNet weights
model <- application_vgg16(input_tensor = input_tensor, weights = "imagenet", 
                           include_top = FALSE)

print("Model loaded.")

nms <- map_chr(model$layers, ~.x$name)
output_dict <- map(model$layers, ~.x$output) %>% set_names(nms)

# compute the neural style loss
# first we need to define 4 util functions

# the gram matrix of an image tensor (feature-wise outer product)

gram_matrix <- function(x){
  
  features <- x %>%
    k_permute_dimensions(pattern = c(3, 1, 2)) %>%
    k_batch_flatten()
  
  k_dot(features, k_transpose(features))
}

# the "style loss" is designed to maintain
# the style of the reference image in the generated image.
# It is based on the gram matrices (which capture style) of
# feature maps from the style reference image
# and from the generated image

style_loss <- function(style, combination){
  S <- gram_matrix(style)
  C <- gram_matrix(combination)
  
  channels <- 3
  size <- img_nrows*img_ncols
  
  k_sum(k_square(S - C)) / (4 * channels^2  * size^2)
}

# an auxiliary loss function
# designed to maintain the "content" of the
# base image in the generated image

content_loss <- function(base, combination){
  k_sum(k_square(combination - base))
}

# the 3rd loss function, total variation loss,
# designed to keep the generated image locally coherent

total_variation_loss <- function(x){
  y_ij  <- x[,1:(img_nrows - 1L), 1:(img_ncols - 1L),]
  y_i1j <- x[,2:(img_nrows), 1:(img_ncols - 1L),]
  y_ij1 <- x[,1:(img_nrows - 1L), 2:(img_ncols),]
  
  a <- k_square(y_ij - y_i1j)
  b <- k_square(y_ij - y_ij1)
  k_sum(k_pow(a + b, 1.25))
}

# combine these loss functions into a single scalar
loss <- k_variable(0.0)
layer_features <- output_dict$block4_conv2
base_image_features <- layer_features[1,,,]
combination_features <- layer_features[3,,,]

loss <- loss + content_weight*content_loss(base_image_features, 
                                           combination_features)

feature_layers = c('block1_conv1', 'block2_conv1',
                  'block3_conv1', 'block4_conv1',
                  'block5_conv1')

for(layer_name in feature_layers){
  layer_features <- output_dict[[layer_name]]
  style_reference_features <- layer_features[2,,,]
  combination_features <- layer_features[3,,,]
  sl <- style_loss(style_reference_features, combination_features)
  loss <- loss + ((style_weight / length(feature_layers)) * sl)
}

loss <- loss + (total_variation_weight * total_variation_loss(combination_image))

# get the gradients of the generated image wrt the loss
grads <- k_gradients(loss, combination_image)[[1]]

f_outputs <- k_function(list(combination_image), list(loss, grads))

eval_loss_and_grads <- function(image){
  image <- array_reshape(image, c(1, img_nrows, img_ncols, 3))
  outs <- f_outputs(list(image))
  list(
    loss_value = outs[[1]],
    grad_values = array_reshape(outs[[2]], dim = length(outs[[2]]))
  )
}

# Loss and gradients evaluator.
# 
# This Evaluator class makes it possible
# to compute loss and gradients in one pass
# while retrieving them via two separate functions,
# "loss" and "grads". This is done because scipy.optimize
# requires separate functions for loss and gradients,
# but computing them separately would be inefficient.
Evaluator <- R6Class(
  "Evaluator",
  public = list(
    
    loss_value = NULL,
    grad_values = NULL,
    
    initialize = function() {
      self$loss_value <- NULL
      self$grad_values <- NULL
    },
    
    loss = function(x){
      loss_and_grad <- eval_loss_and_grads(x)
      self$loss_value <- loss_and_grad$loss_value
      self$grad_values <- loss_and_grad$grad_values
      self$loss_value
    },
    
    grads = function(x){
      grad_values <- self$grad_values
      self$loss_value <- NULL
      self$grad_values <- NULL
      grad_values
    }
    
  )
)

evaluator <- Evaluator$new()

# run scipy-based optimization (L-BFGS) over the pixels of the generated image
# so as to minimize the neural style loss
dms <- c(1, img_nrows, img_ncols, 3)
x <- array(data = runif(prod(dms), min = 0, max = 255) - 128, dim = dms)

# Run optimization (L-BFGS) over the pixels of the generated image
# so as to minimize the loss
for(i in 1:iterations){

  # Run L-BFGS
  opt <- optim(
    array_reshape(x, dim = length(x)), fn = evaluator$loss, gr = evaluator$grads, 
    method = "L-BFGS-B",
    control = list(maxit = 15)
  )
  
  # Print loss value
  print(opt$value)
  
  # decode the image
  image <- x <- opt$par
  image <- array_reshape(image, dms)
  
  # plot
  im <- deprocess_image(image)
  a <- as.raster(im)
  plot(a)
  pdf(paste0(base_dir,"/","v2_",i,".pdf"))
  plot(a)
  dev.off()
}

#add function to export image with parameters
```

If someone could help me to fix this, it would be great. I am currently running out of solutions...

Cheers

title: Slow Keras load: 20-40 seconds per model load using load_model_hdf5()
description:
I'm facing issues with `load_model_hdf5()` load times. I have an ensemble of 20 models. The `meta_data` object holds file paths for trained models. I then want to attach the models, such that I may perform predictions like so `predict(meta_data$model_01$model, X)`. Each model has `181,601` parameters and each `hdf5` file is ~2.2MB. I'm using a new macbook pro and `R-3.4.4` and `keras_2.1.5.9001`. Load times are as follows (weirdly there is seem to be an increasing load time with number of models loaded):

    > meta_data = attach_models(meta_data)
    model_01 loaded in 22.22 secs
    model_02 loaded in 22.68 secs
    model_03 loaded in 23.62 secs
    model_04 loaded in 26.28 secs
    model_05 loaded in 25.81 secs
    model_06 loaded in 26.52 secs
    model_07 loaded in 26.48 secs
    model_08 loaded in 29.14 secs

    model_11 loaded in 29.52 secs
    model_12 loaded in 29.81 secs
    model_13 loaded in 30.34 secs
    model_14 loaded in 31.40 secs
    model_15 loaded in 33.02 secs
    model_16 loaded in 32.82 secs
    model_17 loaded in 35.96 secs
    model_18 loaded in 34.03 secs
    model_19 loaded in 34.59 secs
    model_20 loaded in 38.06 secs

The `attach_models()` function simply looks like so:

    attach_models = function(meta_data){
      now = Sys.time()
      for( model_id in names(meta_data) ){
        model_file = meta_data[[model_id]]$model_file
        meta_data[[model_id]]$model = load_model_hdf5(filepath = model_file)
        cat(model_id, " loaded in ", round(Sys.time() - now, 2), " secs\n", sep = "")
        now = Sys.time()
      }
      return(meta_data)
    }

and then as stated, I can do

But, this means that currently loading the ensemble model will be ~10 minutes, before predictions can be made. I have tried using Hadley's `save_rds()` and `read_rds()` and then saving the models in a meta object after training, but that only stores reference to the model and not the model itself.

Is it really that slow or is something wrong?

description:
[val.RData.zip](https://github.com/rstudio/keras/files/2064515/val.RData.zip)
I trained a model while using both callback_reduce_lr_on_plateau() and
callback_early_stopping().  When I later tried to plot the training history,
I received a warning saying:

```
   Warning message:
   In rbind(values, pad_data) :
     number of columns of result is not a multiple of vector length (arg 2)
```

Some traceback info:

```
   > options(warn=2)
   > plot(val)
   Error in rbind(values, pad_data) : 
     (converted from warning) number of columns of result is not a multiple of vector length (arg 2)
   
   Enter a frame number, or 0 to exit   
   
    1: plot(val)
    2: plot.keras_training_history(val)
    3: as.data.frame(x)
    4: as.data.frame.keras_training_history(x)
    5: rbind(values, pad_data)
    6: .signalSimpleWarning("number of columns of result is not a multiple of vector le
    7: withRestarts({
       .Internal(.signalCondition(simpleWarning(msg, call), msg, cal
    8: withOneRestart(expr, restarts[[1]])
    9: doWithOneRestart(return(expr), restart)
   10: dtk.recover
```
   
In plot.keras_training_history(), it does the following:

```
    ...
    pad_data <- list()
    for (metric in x$params$metrics) pad_data[[metric]] <- rep_len(NA, 
        pad)
    values <- rbind(values, pad_data)
```

At that point in the code I see that x$params$metrics has just 4
values, while x$metrics has 5 named components, and that triggers the
rbind() warning:

```

```

I think if the goal is for learning rate/lr to be plotted along with
the other metrics, the for() loop might need to change to iterate over
all five when constructing the padding, like this:

`    for (metric in names(x$metrics) pad_data[[metric]] <- rep_len(NA, 
[val.RData.zip](https://github.com/rstudio/keras/files/2064507/val.RData.zip)
`

Alternatively, if it should not be plotting lr, some other fix is
required?

If I start R and call use_session_with_seed() first thing in my

    layer_dense(units = 100, activation = "relu") %>%

title: virtualenv path support (little suggestion)
description:
I just spent some time wrestling with a server to get it to run `Keras for R`. The server already has GPU-enabled `tensorflow` set up so this was a bit surprising. It was also surprising that it was more difficult than just running a `tensorflow` session from `R`. I suggest either allowing `install_keras` to accept a `path` to a desired `virtualenv` or adding a little something to the documentation so that users know where to set up their `virtualenv`. 

Here are a few details behind the idea and hopefully a few tips for folks triaging ... 

The issue turned out to be that when `install_keras` setup the `virtualenv`, that `virtualenv` and went ahead found a copy of `python2.6` (presumably by first bellowing "quantum leap"). Since `python2.6` isn't really supported by `pip` anymore, it was downhill from there... 

```
module load tensorflow     # load server's gpu tf along with associated python2.7 
 
virtualenv .virtualenvs/r-tensorflow        
# hidden folder where library(keras) will look for keras. 
# Do not use keras::install_keras()

source .virtualenvs/r-tensorflow/bin/activate
 
pip install keras               # unless keras > 2 is a module
pip install utils np_utils   # don’t think others are needed…
 
R     # above bash, below R
 
require(tensorflow)
require(reticulate)
require(keras)
 
is_keras_available()        # if TRUE, you’re done
 
system(“which python”)
# /opt/rh/python27/root/usr/bin/python
 
Sys.setenv(TENSORFLOW_PYTHON=”/opt/rh/python27/root/usr/bin/python”)
use_python(“/opt/rh/python27/root/usr/bin/python”)          # do both
 
py_discover_config("tensorflow")    # should display appropriate paths for TF,  numpy, etc.
py_discover_config("keras")
 
is_keras_available()        # if TRUE, you’re done
 
# if FALSE, the easiest way to see what’s failing seems to be:
 
reticulate:::import(“keras”)
```

It's not really a problem for my model, as it runs now, however i don't have the value of the dice coefficient during the training and  would like to know if their is an alternative solution to keep/save the value of the dice coefficient on the validation sample somewhere else than this print in the console or maybe if this is possible to desactivate the loading bar and only print the dice coefficient for training and validation sample at the end of each epoch.

title: layer_lambda called twice with different inputs
description:
Hello,
I'm trying to make a layer lambda and I'm running into some curious issues. I'm not sure I'm just not understanding how this is supposed to work, or if this is bug.

My understanding is that the function passed to `layer_lambda` is called once when `layer_lambda` is first evaluated, and that that function is supposed to construct nodes on the tensorflow graph.

However, in this example, the function seems to be called twice. That on it's own is curious but not that important. What's important is that the type of the tensors it's called with the second time is different, and that's causing an error if a certain input type is expected.

Here is a minimal example:
``` r
library(tensorflow)
library(keras)
print_vars <- TKutils::print_vars # just prints the deparsed name before printing the value

input <- layer_input(shape = c(128, 2), dtype = 'float32')

input.complex <- input %>%
  layer_lambda(function(x) {
    cmplx.out <- tf$complex(real = x[, , 1], imag = x[, , 2])
    print_vars(x, cmplx.out)
    cmplx.out
  })
#> x:
#> Tensor("input_1:0", shape=(?, 128, 2), dtype=float32)
#> cmplx.out:
#> Tensor("lambda_1/Complex:0", shape=(?, 128), dtype=complex64)
#> x:
#> Tensor("lambda_1/Placeholder:0", shape=(?, 128, 2), dtype=float32)
#> cmplx.out:
#> Tensor("lambda_1/Complex_1:0", shape=(?, 128), dtype=complex64)

print_vars(input.complex)
#> input.complex:
#> Tensor("lambda_1/Complex:0", shape=(?, 128), dtype=complex64)

fft.res <- input.complex %>%
  layer_lambda(function(x) {
    print_vars(x)
    fft.out <- tf$fft(x)
    print_vars(fft.out)
    fft.out
  })
#> x:
#> Tensor("lambda_1/Complex:0", shape=(?, 128), dtype=complex64)
#> fft.out:
#> Tensor("lambda_2/FFT:0", shape=(?, 128), dtype=complex64)

As there isn't yet any examples of object detection work in keras for Rstudio, I have trained a couple of keras models in python.  Now I would like to use those models for inference (object detection) in Rstudio.  The models were created from the ssd_300/512 models ported to keras (python) at ([https://github.com/pierluigiferrari/ssd_keras](https://github.com/pierluigiferrari/ssd_keras)) which uses some custom layers and modules described in python scripts:

from keras_loss_function.keras_ssd_loss import SSDLoss
from keras_layers.keras_layer_AnchorBoxes import AnchorBoxes

from keras_layers.keras_layer_DecodeDetections2 import DecodeDetections2
from keras_layers.keras_layer_L2Normalization import L2Normalization
```
When attempting to load the saved models in rstudio:
```
library(keras)
myModel<-load_model_hdf5('./models/ssd300_pascal_07+12_finetuned_kitti_model_65e_22638_steps.h5')
```
I get the following error:

```
4. stop(structure(list(message = "ValueError: Unknown layer: L2Normalization",

title: cyclegan layerconcat
description:
I'm converting a cyclegan code written in keras (python) to keras (r), but I do not know how to change this part. Especially Upsampling part.

def build_generator(self):
        """U-Net Generator"""

        def conv2d(layer_input, filters, f_size=4):
            """Layers used during downsampling"""
            d = Conv2D(filters, kernel_size=f_size, strides=2, padding='same')(layer_input)
            d = LeakyReLU(alpha=0.2)(d)
            d = InstanceNormalization()(d)
            return d

        def deconv2d(layer_input, skip_input, filters, f_size=4, dropout_rate=0):
            """Layers used during upsampling"""
            u = UpSampling2D(size=2)(layer_input)
            u = Conv2D(filters, kernel_size=f_size, strides=1, padding='same', activation='relu')(u)
            if dropout_rate:
                u = Dropout(dropout_rate)(u)
            u = InstanceNormalization()(u)
            u = Concatenate()([u, skip_input])
            return u

        # Image input
        d0 = Input(shape=self.img_shape)

        # Downsampling
        d1 = conv2d(d0, self.gf)
        d2 = conv2d(d1, self.gf*2)
        d3 = conv2d(d2, self.gf*4)
        d4 = conv2d(d3, self.gf*8)

        # Upsampling
        u1 = deconv2d(d4, d3, self.gf*4)
        u2 = deconv2d(u1, d2, self.gf*2)
        u3 = deconv2d(u2, d1, self.gf)

        u4 = UpSampling2D(size=2)(u3)
        output_img = Conv2D(self.channels, kernel_size=4, strides=1, padding='same', activation='tanh')(u4)

title: kl_loss in vae example implementation

kl_loss <- -0.5*k_mean(1 + z_log_var - k_square(z_mean) - k_exp(z_log_var), axis = -1L)
Pretty sure this should be:
kl_loss <- -0.5*k_mean(1 + 2*z_log_var - k_square(z_mean) - k_exp(z_log_var), axis = -1L)

I know this is the same formula used in the python implementation so probably this small error propagated from there?

title: fit_generator() more than twice as slow as fit()
description:
Hello, I noticed that `fit_generator()` is significantly slower than `fit()`. I'm not sure if this is surprising behavior, or if it's an inevitable fact of life due to the overhead between calling an R function from python. I'm hopeful that there is some easy optimization that can put these two functions on equal footing. 

Here is an example with some dummy data and a minimal keras model. 

``` r
library(keras)

batch_size = 1024
steps_per_epoch = 1000
d = c(batch_size * steps_per_epoch, 128, 2)
X <- array(rnorm(prod(d)), d)
Y <- matrix(0, nrow = nrow(X), ncol = 10)
Y[cbind(seq_len(nrow(X)), sample(10, nrow(X), replace = TRUE ))] <- 1

new_model <- function() {
  keras_model_sequential() %>%
    layer_flatten( input = c(128, 2)) %>%
    layer_dense(10, use_bias = FALSE, activation = 'softmax') %>%
    compile(optimizer = 'adam', loss = 'mae')
}

new_data_generator <- function() {
  start <- 1L
  function() {
    end <- start + batch_size - 1L
    idx <- start:end
    if(end > nrow(X)) {
      over <- idx > nrow(X)
      idx[over] <- seq_len(sum(over))
    }

    on.exit(start <<- idx[batch_size] + 1L)
    list(X[idx,,], Y[idx,])
  }
}

generator <-  new_data_generator()

model <- new_model()
fit_timing <- system.time(fit(model, x = X, y = Y, batch_size = batch_size,
                              epochs = 3, verbose = 1))

model <- new_model()
fit_generator_timing <- system.time(fit_generator(model, generator = generator,
                          steps_per_epoch = steps_per_epoch, epochs = 3, verbose = 1))

fit_timing
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>  12.521   1.592   8.737
fit_generator_timing
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>  25.036   1.587  20.269
```

title: Custom loss function for Weibull log-likelihood
description:
Hi,

I'm trying to convert the python loss function from this repo:
https://github.com/daynebatten/keras-wtte-rnn

```
weibull_loglik_discrete = function(y_true, y_pred) {
  K = backend()
  y_true = K$eval(y_true)
  y_pred = K$eval(y_pred)
  y_ = y_true[, 1]
  u_ = y_true[, 2]
  a_ = y_pred[, 1]
  b_ = y_pred[, 2]

  hazard0 = ((y_ + 1e-35) / a_) ^ b_
  hazard1 = ((y_ + 1) / a_) ^ b_

  return(K$constant(-1 * mean(u_ * log(exp(hazard1 - hazard0) - 1.0) - hazard1), dtype = 'float', shape = 1))
}

weibull_activate = function(ab) {
  a = k_exp(ab[, 1])
  b = k_softplus(ab[, 2])
  
  a = k_reshape(a, c(length(a), 1))
  b = k_reshape(b, c(length(b), 1))
  
  return(k_concatenate(list(a, b)))

description:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/628977/38459230-4380d270-3a75-11e8-972d-4d835e6e0197.png)

The minimal code to reproduce this is as follows.

```R
library(mxnet)
library(keras)
{
    mnist <- dataset_mnist()
    train_images <- mnist$train$x
    train_labels <- mnist$train$y
    test_images <- mnist$test$x
    test_labels <- mnist$test$y
    train_labels <- to_categorical(train_labels)
    test_labels <- to_categorical(test_labels)
    
    train_images <- array_reshape(train_images, c(60000, 28 * 28))
    train_images <- train_images / 255
    test_images <- array_reshape(test_images, c(10000, 28 * 28))
    test_images <- test_images / 255
}

k_clear_session()
network <- keras_model_sequential() %>% 
    layer_dense(units = 512, activation = "relu", input_shape = c(28 * 28)) %>% 
    layer_dense(units = 10, activation = "softmax")

network %>% 
    compile(  optimizer = "rmsprop", 
              loss = "categorical_crossentropy", 
              metrics = c("accuracy")

network %>%

title: predict() for image larger than used in training
description:
Hi,

I am using the get_unet_128 model from the rstudio keras examples in linux [here](https://keras.rstudio.com/articles/examples/unet_linux.html)
The function predict() works with the model for image of size 128 x 128 , however i don't manage to make prediction with this model on larger image (i.e. 2048 x 2048). For remote sensing applications, it's important as i dont want to cut all images that will be used only for prediction in small tiles. One [issue](https://github.com/keras-team/keras/issues/3267) is related to this in keras but the parameter check_input_shapes of the python function predict() does not exist in the r function predict(). 

the error message is : 
Error in py_call_impl(callable, dots$args, dots$keywords) : 
  ValueError: Error when checking : expected input_1 to have shape (128, 128, 3) but got array with shape (2048, 2048, 3) 

Any help is welcome !

Thank you very much,

Fabien

title: Support specifying the number of workers to use in predict_generator
description:
See `predict_generator` at https://keras.io/models/model/#methods:
`predict_generator(self, generator, steps=None, max_queue_size=10, workers=1, use_multiprocessing=False, verbose=0)`

`workers` specifies the maximum number of processes to spin up. Being able to specify multiple workers is very useful to perform image preprocessing and/or data augmentation on multiple CPUs and keep the GPU busy.

description:
Using keras with R 3.4.4 in Windows 10, I notice that deleting a keras model with rm() does not free up the memory used by R, according to Task Manager. I have also tried garbage collection, gc(), and it does not help. For example, after running

```
library(keras)
mnist <- dataset_mnist()
x_train <- mnist$train$x
y_train <- mnist$train$y
x_test <- mnist$test$x
y_test <- mnist$test$y
x_train <- array_reshape(x_train, c(nrow(x_train), 784))
x_test <- array_reshape(x_test, c(nrow(x_test), 784))

x_train <- x_train / 255
x_test <- x_test / 255
y_train <- to_categorical(y_train, 10)
y_test <- to_categorical(y_test, 10)
model <- keras_model_sequential() 
model %>% 
  layer_dense(units = 500, activation = 'relu', input_shape = c(784)) %>% 
  layer_dropout(rate = 0.4) %>% 
  layer_dense(units = 500, activation = 'relu') %>%
  layer_dropout(rate = 0.3) %>%
  layer_dense(units = 10, activation = 'softmax')
```

Windows Task Manager reports that R is using 1271.8MB. After running this loop

```
for(i in 1:1000){

title: text_to_sequences only encodes characters
description:

```

                                   y_pred <- self$model$predict(self$validation_data[[1]])
                                   score = AUC::roc(labels = self$validation_data[[2]], predictions = y_pred)
                                   print(paste("ROC_AUC for epoch", epoch, "=", score))
                             }    
                       ))

auc_roc_metric <- auc_roc$new()
history <- model1 %>% fit(x = X_train, y = Y_train,

                          validation_data = list(x_valid, y_valid),

```

I get following error

` y_pred <- self$model$predict(self$validation_data[1], steps = self$params$batch_size)`

label = c('toxic', 'severe_toxic', 'obscene', 'threat', 'insult', 'identity_hate')

train_text <- data.frame(comments = raw_data$comment_text, stringsAsFactors = F)

            if (i %% 1000 == 0) {

                          batch_size = 128, epochs = 2,
                          validation_data = list(x_valid, y_valid), 
                          callbacks = list(auc_roc_metric, callback_early_stopping(patience = 3, mode = "max")))

print("Predicting test data...")
system.time(test_preds <- as.data.frame(predict(model1, X_test)))
colnames(test_preds) <- label
submissions <- read.csv("Data/sample_submission.csv", stringsAsFactors = F)
test_preds$id <- submissions$id

print("Writing csv file!")
write.csv(test_preds, paste0("results/",glove_file,format(Sys.time(), "%Y_%m_%d_%H_%M_%S"),".csv"), row.names = F)
```

title: Overparameterized separable convolution error
description:
I have found quite strange behavior of `layer_separable_conv_2d`.

    input <- layer_input(shape = c(256, 256, 3))
    out<- input %>% 
        layer_conv_2d(filters = 64, kernel_size = c(1, 1), padding='same', activation='relu') %>%
        layer_separable_conv_2d(filters = 64, kernel_size = c(3, 3), depth_multiplier = 2, activation='relu')

This code produces an error:
    
     Error in py_call_impl(callable, dots$args, dots$keywords) : 
     ValueError: Refusing to perform an overparameterized separable convolution: channel_multiplier *   
     in_channels = 2 * 64 = 128 > 64 = out_channels 
 
But we surely can expand future map from 64 to 128 layers at depthwise step (`depth_multiplier = 2`) and 
then reduce it back to 64 (`filters = 64`) (or set to arbitrary number) with 1x1 convolutions.
It looks like old constraint of TF that was already removed as pointed in https://stackoverflow.com/questions/45193238/why-out-channels-must-be-greater-then-channel-multiplier-in-channels-in-pointw

Thanks for your help

title: keras_model_sequential() crashes Rsession
description:
I'm trying to install Keras with gpu in R,following instructions posted [here](https://keras.rstudio.com/reference/install_keras.html). After a successful install , when I try to build a model using keras_model_sequential(), my R session crashes. My system info can be viewed [here](https://i.stack.imgur.com/XfQ0F.png).

 I'm running CUDA 9.0 with CuDNN version 7.0.5, tensorflow version 1.5.0-gpu and have set the requisite path variables in ~/.profile . Can someone please help me fix this ?

description:
I am running the code from the book Deep Learning with R. The code in the second chapter gives a different values of the following quantities:
$loss
[1] 0.07519608
$acc
[1] 0.9785

My values are:
$loss
[1] 0.07382395

$acc
[1] 0.9768

Now my question is whether there could be a slight variation every time we run a code in keras?

title: How to use custom constraints?
description:
In Python this is pretty simple, make a class that extends `keras.constraints.Constraint` and implement the `__call__` method.

However, I can't see how to do the same in R, as the Constraint objects that are returned by the `constraint_<x>` functions subclass from both `keras.constraints.Constraint` and `python.builtin.object`. And the [source code](https://github.com/rstudio/keras/blob/master/R/constraints.R) just seems to directly create Python objects.

Is there any easy way of making a custom constraint without understanding how `reticulate` calls the underlying Python library?

title: Custom layer inheriting other layers
description:
I would like to implement a custom layer based on an existing layer, for example the python code is:

```
class DependentDense(Dense):
    def __init__(self, output_dim, master_layer, init='glorot_uniform', activation='linear', weights=None,
                 W_regularizer=None, b_regularizer=None, activity_regularizer=None,
                 W_constraint=None, b_constraint=None, input_dim=None, **kwargs):
        self.master_layer = master_layer
        super().__init__(output_dim, **kwargs)

    def build(self):
        self.W = self.master_layer.W.T
        self.b = K.zeros((self.output_dim,))
        self.params = [self.b]
        self.regularizers = []
        if self.W_regularizer:
            self.W_regularizer.set_param(self.W)
            self.regularizers.append(self.W_regularizer)

        if self.b_regularizer:
            self.b_regularizer.set_param(self.b)
            self.regularizers.append(self.b_regularizer)

        if self.activity_regularizer:
            self.activity_regularizer.set_layer(self)
            self.regularizers.append(self.activity_regularizer)

        if self.initial_weights is not None:
            self.set_weights(self.initial_weights)
            del self.initial_weights
```

This is, I will only modify `init` and `build` methods. @jjallaire  do you think this is actually possible?

Best,
Daniel

    model = Sequential()
    model.add(Dense(units=64, activation='relu', input_dim=100))
    model.add(Dense(units=10, activation='softmax'))
    model.compile(loss='categorical_crossentropy',
              optimizer='sgd',
              metrics=['accuracy'])

    return model


def train_and_evaluate__model(model, data[train], labels[train], data[test], labels[test)):
    model.fit...

if __name__ == "__main__":
    n_folds = 10
    data, labels, header_info = load_data()
    skf = StratifiedKFold(labels, n_folds=n_folds, shuffle=True)

    for i, (train, test) in enumerate(skf):
            print "Running Fold", i+1, "/", n_folds

title: On use of layer_batch_normalization
description:
Consider the following example:

```
library(keras)

# since we are using stateful rnn tsteps can be set to 1
tsteps <- 1
batch_size <- 25
epochs <- 25
# number of elements ahead that are used to make the prediction
lahead <- 1

# Generates an absolute cosine time series with the amplitude exponentially decreasing
# Arguments:
#   amp: amplitude of the cosine function
#   period: period of the cosine function
#   x0: initial x of the time series
#   xn: final x of the time series
#   step: step of the time series discretization
#   k: exponential rate
gen_cosine_amp <- function(amp = 100, period = 1000, x0 = 0, xn = 50000, step = 1, k = 0.0001) {
  n <- (xn-x0) * step
  cos <- array(data = numeric(n), dim = c(n, 1, 1))
  for (i in 1:length(cos)) {
    idx <- x0 + i * step
    cos[[i, 1, 1]] <- amp * cos(2 * pi * idx / period)
    cos[[i, 1, 1]] <- cos[[i, 1, 1]] * exp(-k * idx)
  }
  cos
}

description:

https://blog.keras.io/keras-as-a-simplified-interface-to-tensorflow-tutorial.html#exporting-a-model-with-tensorflow-serving

title: custom loss metric that mixes multi-output predictions during training
description:
How do we index y_pred during training for multi-output regression problems? As a toy example, consider the prediction of 3 outputs (y1, y2, y3) using one model, and we know that for each observation (i.e, row) y1 < y2 < y3. For simple datasets the model learns this relationship but for real-world examples it often produces non-monotonic outputs. The code below intentionally underfits a model to illustrate the point.

```r
library(keras)
library(tidyverse)

# number of observations
N <- 1000

# synthetic multiple outputs
y1 <- rnorm(N,20,5) # smallest
y2 <- y1 + rnorm(N,7,2) # middle
y3 <- y2 + rnorm(N,7,2) # largest
Y <- data.frame(y1,y2,y3) # combine
Y <- Y * rexp(N,2) # randomly scale rows

# synthetic nonlinear predictors
x1 <- (sqrt(y1) + rnorm(N,0,1))^2
x2 <- log10((x1 + y2)^3)
x3 <- sqrt(abs(y3-y2))
x4 <- sqrt((x1 + y2)^2)

X <- data.frame(x1,x2,x3,x4) %>% # combine
  mutate_all(funs(scale)) %>% # scale
  as.matrix() # to matrix

# create train and test set
set.seed(0)
ind <- sample(2, N, replace=T, prob=c(0.50, 0.50))

Xtrain <- X[ind==1,]
Ytrain <- Y[ind==1,]
Xtest <- X[ind==2,]
Ytest <- Y[ind==2,]

# add covariates
input <- layer_input(shape=dim(X)[2],name="covars")

# add hidden layers
base_model <- input  %>%
  layer_dense(units = 4, activation='relu') 

# add output 1 
yhat1 <- base_model %>% 
  layer_dense(units = 1, name="yhat1") 

# add output 2
yhat2 <- base_model %>% 
  layer_dense(units = 1, name="yhat2") 

# add output 3
yhat3 <- base_model %>% 
  layer_dense(units = 1, name="yhat3")

# caclulate squared weights for mse loss
weight_fun <- function(x){mean(y1/x)}
weights <- as.numeric(apply(Y,2,weight_fun))^2

# build multi-output model
model <- keras_model(input,list(yhat1,yhat2,yhat3)) %>%
  compile(optimizer = "rmsprop",
          loss="mse",
          metrics="mae",
          loss_weights=weights)

# fit model (intentionally underfit)
model_fit <- model %>% 
  fit(x=Xtrain,
      y=list(Ytrain[,1],Ytrain[,2],Ytrain[,3]), 
      epochs=75, 
      batch_size = 25, 
      validation_split = 0.1, 
      verbose=0)

# predict values for test set
Yhat <- predict(model, Xtest) %>%
  data.frame() %>%
  setNames(colnames(Y))

# sum monotonic violations 
sum(apply(Yhat,1,function(x){sum(cummax(x)!=x)}))
sum(apply(Ytest,1,function(x){sum(cummax(x)!=x)}))
```
There will be some number of violations for Yhat and 0 for Ytest. My goal is to create a custom loss that add an error to the MSE that is a scaled-sum of the number of violations of monotonicity. Something like this is close,

```r
# custom loss function
loss_custom <- function(y_true, y_pred){
  val <- k_placeholder(dtype = 'float32')
  mse <- k_placeholder(dtype = 'float32')
  n <- k_placeholder(dtype = 'float32')
  k <- k_placeholder(dtype = 'float32')
  n <- k_shape(y_pred)[[1]]
  k <- k_shape(y_pred)[[2]]
  y_pred <- array_reshape(y_pred,dim=c(k,n))
  y_true <- array_reshape(y_true,dim=c(k,n))
  val <- k_sum(k_cast(k_less(y_pred[2:k]-y_pred[1:k-1],0),'float32'))
  mse <- k_mean(k_square(y_true-y_pred)) 
  return(mse + val)
}
```

The initial errors with the custom loss function are all index related. What shape is y_pred when training a model with multiple outputs? Using `predict` returns a list but that doesn't seem to be the case for y_pred during training. I have a more detailed version of this [question on SO](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/48573269/custom-monotonic-loss-function-multi-output-r-keras), but I think the real issue is acessing and combining the multiple predictions.

title: Error when using Output of custom layer as input to further layer.
description:
Hi, I am trying to implement a custom layer in keras R. I discovered, that you run into an error, when using the Output of a custom layer as the Input of a further layer. As a reproducible example: The Custom layer from the Keras Website: 

```
CustomLayer <- R6::R6Class("CustomLayer",
                           
                           inherit = KerasLayer,
                           
                           public = list(
                             
                             output_dim = NULL,
                             
                             kernel = NULL,
                             
                             initialize = function(output_dim) {
                               self$output_dim <- output_dim
                             },
                             
                             build = function(input_shape) {
                               self$kernel <- self$add_weight(
                                 name = 'kernel', 
                                 shape = list(input_shape[[2]], self$output_dim),
                                 initializer = initializer_random_normal(),
                                 trainable = TRUE
                               )
                             },
                             
                             call = function(x, mask = NULL) {
                               k$dot(x, self$kernel)
                             },
                             
                             compute_output_shape = function(input_shape) {
                               list(input_shape[[1]], self$output_dim)
                             }
                           )
)
# define layer wrapper function
layer_custom <- function(object, output_dim, name = NULL, trainable = TRUE) {
  create_layer(CustomLayer, object, list(
    output_dim = as.integer(output_dim),
    name = name,
    trainable = trainable
  ))
}
```

Now if we set up a Network which uses the Output of the custom layer as an Input: 

```

i=layer_input(shape  =   list(32,32))
d=layer_dense(i,units = 32)
c=layer_custom(d,output_dim = 32)
# Here we use it as an input
c2=layer_dense(c,units = 32)

We get an error:

I suspect it has to do with the difference between tuples and lists as Output shapes. as you can see in the description of the model:

description:
I have the following code. The data set can be downloaded [here][1] or [here][2]. The data set contains images categorized as `cat` or `dog`.

The task of this code is for training cats and dogs image data.
So that given a picture, it can tell whether it's cat's or dog.
It is motivated by this [page][3]. Below is the fully running code:

    library(keras)
    library(tidyverse)
    
    
    # Organize dataset --------------------------------------------------------
    options(warn = -1)
    
    # Ths input
    original_dataset_dir <- "data/kaggle_cats_dogs/original/"
    
    
    # Create new organized dataset directory ----------------------------------
    
    base_dir <- "data/kaggle_cats_dogs_small/"
    dir.create(base_dir)
    
    model_dir <- paste0(base_dir, "model/")
    dir.create(model_dir)
    
    train_dir <- file.path(base_dir, "train")
    dir.create(train_dir)
    
    validation_dir <- file.path(base_dir, "validation")
    dir.create(validation_dir)
    
    test_dir <- file.path(base_dir, "test")
    dir.create(test_dir)
    
    train_cats_dir <- file.path(train_dir, "cats")
    dir.create(train_cats_dir)
    
    train_dogs_dir <- file.path(train_dir, "dogs")
    dir.create(train_dogs_dir)
    
    validation_cats_dir <- file.path(validation_dir, "cats")
    dir.create(validation_cats_dir)
    
    validation_dogs_dir <- file.path(validation_dir, "dogs")
    dir.create(validation_dogs_dir)
    
    test_cats_dir <- file.path(test_dir, "cats")
    dir.create(test_cats_dir)
    
    test_dogs_dir <- file.path(test_dir, "dogs")
    dir.create(test_dogs_dir)
    
    # Copying files from original dataset to newly created directory
    fnames <- paste0("cat.", 1:1000, ".jpg")
    dum <- file.copy(
      file.path(original_dataset_dir, fnames),
      file.path(train_cats_dir)
    )
    
    
    fnames <- paste0("cat.", 1001:1500, ".jpg")
    dum <- file.copy(
      file.path(original_dataset_dir, fnames),
      file.path(validation_cats_dir)
    )
    
    fnames <- paste0("cat.", 1501:2000, ".jpg")
    dum <- file.copy(
      file.path(original_dataset_dir, fnames),
      file.path(test_cats_dir)
    )
    
    fnames <- paste0("dog.", 1:1000, ".jpg")
    dum <- file.copy(
      file.path(original_dataset_dir, fnames),
      file.path(train_dogs_dir)
    )
    
    fnames <- paste0("dog.", 1001:1500, ".jpg")
    dum <- file.copy(
      file.path(original_dataset_dir, fnames),
      file.path(validation_dogs_dir)
    )
    
    fnames <- paste0("dog.", 1501:2000, ".jpg")
    dum <- file.copy(
      file.path(original_dataset_dir, fnames),
      file.path(test_dogs_dir)
    )
    
    options(warn = 0)
    
    # Making model ------------------------------------------------------------
    
    
    conv_base <- application_vgg16(
      weights = "imagenet",
      include_top = FALSE,
      input_shape = c(150, 150, 3)
    )
    
    
    model <- keras_model_sequential() %>%
      conv_base() %>%
      layer_flatten() %>%
      layer_dense(units = 256, activation = "relu") %>%
      layer_dense(units = 1, activation = "sigmoid")
    
    summary(model)
    
    length(model$trainable_weights)
    freeze_weights(conv_base)
    length(model$trainable_weights)
    
    
    
    # Train model -------------------------------------------------------------
    
    train_datagen <- image_data_generator(
      rescale = 1 / 255,
      rotation_range = 40,
      width_shift_range = 0.2,
      height_shift_range = 0.2,
      shear_range = 0.2,
      zoom_range = 0.2,
      horizontal_flip = TRUE,
      fill_mode = "nearest"
    )
    
    # Note that the validation data shouldn't be augmented!
    test_datagen <- image_data_generator(rescale = 1 / 255)
    
    train_generator <- flow_images_from_directory(
      train_dir, # Target directory
      train_datagen, # Data generator
      target_size = c(150, 150), # Resizes all images to 150 × 150
      shuffle = FALSE,
      batch_size = 20,
      class_mode = "binary" # binary_crossentropy loss for binary labels
    )
    
    test_generator <- flow_images_from_directory(
      test_dir, # Target directory
      train_datagen, # Data generator
      target_size = c(150, 150), # Resizes all images to 150 × 150
      shuffle = FALSE,
      batch_size = 20,
      class_mode = "binary" # binary_crossentropy loss for binary labels
    )
    
    validation_generator <- flow_images_from_directory(
      validation_dir,
      test_datagen,
      target_size = c(150, 150),
      shuffle = FALSE,
      batch_size = 20,
      class_mode = "binary"
    )
    
    
    # Fine tuning -------------------------------------------------------------
    
    
    unfreeze_weights(conv_base, from = "block3_conv1")
    
    # Compile model -----------------------------------------------------------
    
    
    
    model %>% compile(
      loss = "binary_crossentropy",
      optimizer = optimizer_rmsprop(lr = 2e-5),
      metrics = c("accuracy")
    )
    
    
    # Evaluate  by epochs  ---------------------------------------------------------------
    
    #  # This create plots accuracy of various epochs (slow)
    history <- model %>% fit_generator(
      train_generator,
      steps_per_epoch = 100,
      epochs = 50, # was 50
      validation_data = validation_generator,
      validation_steps = 50
    )

Evaluation gives the following great result:

    > model %>% evaluate_generator(test_generator, steps = 50)
    $loss
    [1] 0.262562
    
    $acc
    [1] 0.923

But then, I tried to 'manually' check the prediction accuracy the following way

    predict <- model %>%
      predict_generator(test_generator, step = 50, verbose = 1)

    # Eye-ball check the prediction
    # Essentially predict_proba is the probability of the image being dog
    stat_df <- as.tibble(cbind(predict, test_generator$filenames, test_generator$classes)) %>%
      rename(
        predict_proba = V1,
        filename = V2,
        test_label = V3
      ) %>%
      mutate(predicted_label = ifelse(predict_proba > 0.5, 1, 0)) %>%
      # sample_n(size= 20) %>% 
      mutate(predicted_label = as.integer(predicted_label)) %>%
      mutate(predicted_label_name = ifelse(predicted_label == 0, "cats", "dogs")) %>%
      separate(filename, into=c("true_label","fname"), sep = "[//]" )
    
    
        stat_df %>% head()
    # A tibble: 6 x 6
    #         predict_proba true_label        fname test_label predicted_label predicted_label_name
    #                 <chr>      <chr>        <chr>      <chr>           <int>                <chr>
    # 1 3.82422604161547e-06       cats cat.1501.jpg          0               1                 dogs
    # 2 7.63378269391404e-18       cats cat.1502.jpg          0               1                 dogs
    # 3 5.30394572706427e-07       cats cat.1503.jpg          0               1                 dogs
    # 4 5.94179291934537e-19       cats cat.1504.jpg          0               1                 dogs
    # 5 8.22905276436359e-05       cats cat.1505.jpg          0               1                 dogs
    # 6 0.000384396902518347       cats cat.1506.jpg          0               0                 cats
    
Proportion of predicted label

    > stat_df %>% group_by(predicted_label_name) %>% summarise(n=n())
    # A tibble: 2 x 2
      predicted_label_name     n
                     <chr> <int>
    1                 cats   197
    2                 dogs   803
        
 Number of prediction correctly predicted as dog or cat:
 

    > stat_df %>% filter(true_label == predicted_label_name & true_label == "dogs")  %>% dim()
    [1] 432   6
    > stat_df %>% filter(true_label == predicted_label_name & true_label == "cats")  %>% dim()
    [1] 129   6

Which says that out of 803 prediction only 432 is correctly predicted as dogs (that's around 54% accuracy). Why is that? Where did I go wrong?

Note that the `evaluate_generator()` gives around 92% accuracy. What's the correct interpretation?

How can I resolve the difference?

  [1]: https://www.dropbox.com/s/qjt5o31oyqj10m8/data.tar.gz?dl=0
  [2]: https://www.kaggle.com/c/dogs-vs-cats/data
  [3]: https://tensorflow.rstudio.com/blog/keras-image-classification-on-small-datasets.html
